https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c84g: Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.
Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty. The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.
After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".
In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future".

"Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.
The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.
The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles (209 km) from the Falkland Islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting from the oilfield within two years, potentially generating huge revenues for the roughly 3,500 inhabitants of the islands.

But the Argentinian government claimed the marine environment of disputed maritime areas is protected by international law, arguing that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.

The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.
The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nations' sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".

It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening . The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.
"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.
The 10-week war that was fought in 1982 started when Argentine forces landed on the Falklands to stake a territorial claim over the islands, as a British military task force fought to eject them.
The conflict led to the deaths of 255 British military personnel, three islanders and 649 Argentine military personnel.
Despite its defeat, Argentina has always maintained its right to the Falklands, and over the years, successive governments have pressed their claim with varying degrees of aggression and diplomacy.
The UK government has made clear that sovereignty remains with Britain and maintains that the island's population has a right to self-determination.
In a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm5y: Médecins Sans Frontières says the number of its staff who have been killed in Gaza has risen to 17
Two workers for the medical charity Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.
MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.
The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".
In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "​Our premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."
In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".
The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".
Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.
Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.

Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.
Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.
"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.
He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.
The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.
Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8: At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told the BBC.
The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.
Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.

The province's culture and information director Sami ul Haq Bayan said the blast took place in a house near Shagai Middle School in Asadabad as explosives were being prepared for mining and blasting rock, reports AFP.
The Associated Press also cites the official saying up to 15 wounded people remain in hospital, while the rest have been discharged after treatment.
Pictures from inside a damaged classroom show shattered glass and debris surrounding abandoned shoes and school bags.
Footage shared on social media showed several wounded children being taken out of cars and carried into the emergency department at a hospital in Asadabad as a large crowd watched on.
Children rushed to hospital following deadly Afghan school explosion
Photos from inside the hospital also show children lying next to each other in hospital beds with bandages strapped around their heads.
Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan but safety standards are often poor, leading to accidents.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8wy: Pedro Sánchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politics
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.

Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
Alberto Núñez Feijóo's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls

The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.

Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
Abascal said on Friday that Sánchez's government had 'betrayed' Spaniards

If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".

Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
Leaders clash in final Spain election debate as housing dominates run-in
Clashing political visions reflect a divided Spain ahead of election
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.

All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.

While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm15: ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.
Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.
OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".
The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".
OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.
Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".
A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.
OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (£4.7bn) deal.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9: A Peruvian military helicopter crashed during a rescue mission
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.
Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.
The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.
In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".
It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".
The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.
No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".
In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.
Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine , according to the United Nations.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmx2: The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.
Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.
He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.
During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.
If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.
As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".
"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.
Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."
He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims
Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.
At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.
"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."
The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.
Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.
Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c820: Watch: Zelensky questions "strange" Trump-Putin friendship in BBC interview

Volodymyr Zelensky has voiced deep frustration with the US, criticising Donald Trump for calling Vladimir Putin "my friend" and saying delays in delivering vital anti-ballistic missiles were costing Ukrainian lives.

In an interview with the BBC at his central Kyiv office, Ukraine's president complained the US was not pushing Russia hard enough in peace talks, and called it "strange" that Trump posted a photo of himself embracing Putin.
"Of course it's up to the president of the United States, but... it's strange," Zelensky said, speaking in English.
"He's an aggressor, and a killer... He can't be a friend. Just cannot be," he said, adding it was like saying you were friends with Adolf Hitler during World War Two.
Since a bruising encounter with Trump in the Oval Office in 2025, Zelensky has been careful how he handles relations with the US.

Trump's two envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, have been trying to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine - to end the huge loss of life. But they often seem more in tune with Moscow's position, than that of Kyiv.
Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, said on Wednesday that Putin had shown "restraint" by not using nuclear weapons in Ukraine. He also described Putin as a "grand master of politics".
The latest round of peace talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this month made no obvious progress: "The more we know, the more problems", is how Zelensky described it.

On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social platform that at his own summit with Putin in China last week he had urged Russia to "pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe" and said he believed a peace deal with Ukraine was "a strong possibility".
But from its public statements, Russia appears to have regressed to its initial, hardline negotiating positions – on everything.
And Zelensky revealed that it was not clear whether European negotiators would be at the table, as the US envoys had announced .
Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
Ukraine urgently needs the talks to move forward and bring five exhausting years of Russia's full-scale invasion to an end.
Russian strikes across the country have been growing more frequent and more deadly: the number of civilians being killed is at an all-time high.
So Zelensky called for "real helpful allies, who can push Russia" to achieve results and urged the US to live up to its reputation as a strong country with "power and respect".
"When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor... it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It's not right," he said.
The US argues that it is neutral: in the complex search for a peace deal between the two sides that can hold.
Questioned again on Thursday about calling Putin a friend, Trump told reporters: "We want to stop killing. I could say he's not a friend... I want to make a deal."
He added: "I could walk in and say, I don't like you, and then we have the same problem that we have with Zelensky and Putin.
"You know... the biggest problem to that settlement is the fact that you have two leaders that really hate each other."

The air alerts, day and night, are now a draining feature of everyday life. As Russian ballistic missiles target power stations and bridges, jet-powered drones are launched daily at central Kyiv and other big cities.
Ukraine launches hundreds of drones at targets in Russia in response.
Zelensky said the military here are now able to destroy about 70% of Russia's fastest drones, a statistic he said was improving.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckd7: Since New York City officials postponed the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, a precaution ahead of a storm that brought heavy rain, wind and flooding, hundreds of touring performers who traveled from across the US to perform were thrust into chaos.
"It was jarring," said Ryan Demkovich, director of a Texas high school marching band. After learning the news, he had to scramble to make new arrangements for over 500 people.
Demkovich and his Pearland High School band made the quick decision to launch a fundraiser, reaching $350,000 (£267,000) in just a few hours.
Still, some performers reportedly had to skip the parade, a televised, traditional Thanksgiving event - now rescheduled for Saturday.
On Wednesday afternoon, a day before the event, organisers announced the postponement, in part due to concerns around the parade's giant balloons in strong winds.
The balloons, inflated on Wednesday, were then temporarily deflated - along with the spirits of those who journeyed to the city to watch the action.
The move represented the first time the event had been postponed in its 100-year history, although it was suspended altogether during World War II.

Each year, a number of marching bands travel from across the country, from high schools and colleges, to perform at the event. This is considered a huge opportunity, as the parade is watched by millions in person and on TV.
Hundreds of thousands still without power after storms hit US on Thanksgiving
Demkovich described an emotional and exhausting experience, first learning that the parade would be postponed while watching a Broadway performance of Wicked with his band.
"My initial thought was like, 'Oh, crap. We're not going to be able to go'," he said.
"Where are we going to be able to get all the money for this?"
The delay meant unexpected expenses of additional nights in a hotel - and meals - for hundreds of people in the middle of New York City during the holidays.
There were no vacancies to extend their stay at the New York Marriott Marquis in Times Square, so they booked the nearest hotel with availability - across the Hudson River - in New Jersey.
Demkovich said the Pride of Pearland Marching Band posted a fundraiser online and within hours met its fundraising goal.
"The word just spread like wildfire, truly like wildfire," Demkovich said, adding that donations came from over 2,000 people and local businesses.
He called the outpouring of support "very, very overwhelming to think about and comprehend".
Some groups were not able to maneuver as easily. The University of Alabama's Million Dollar Band is one of those missing out, due to a schedule conflict on Saturday.
“‘This can’t be happening’,” Rina Browder, mother of a snare drummer in the band, told local news, describing the band’s reactions.
"They were devastated. They've worked so hard for this. So many practices."
The Pride of Pearland Marching Band from Texas - pictured rehearsing earlier this week - said it raised hundreds of thousands of dollars

Meanwhile, a group from Hawaii, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band, said it too would still be able to participate in the parade, also because of emergency fundraising by families, friends and other supporters donating more than $500,000.
Speaking to the BBC on Thursday, the group's director Rickey H Badua described the time pressures. "We are racing to get this done," he explained.
The band is made up of hundreds of musicians from dozens of schools across the state. It travelled almost 5,000 miles (8,000km) to get to New York.
"Getting the news that we got the parade postponed was not easy, and emotional for our students," Badua said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq3d: Canada's top court has largely upheld a Quebec law banning public sector workers from wearing religious symbols, including the hijab and the cross.
The law, known as Bill 21, faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers, who argued it violated their fundamental rights.

Quebec passed the law in 2019 under a unique fixture of Canada's constitution called the "notwithstanding clause" - a legal loophole that allows governments to override certain rights, like freedom of religion.
The Supreme Court's decision is one of the most closely watched in Canadian history, with an impact that will be felt both in Quebec and across the country.

Reacting to the ruling on CBC, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government would study its implications, adding it was important for all legislatures "to respect the rights and liberties of all Canadians, including those in the minority."

The Supreme Court was asked to weigh in on a number of questions, including on the constitutionality of Bill 21, whether Quebec's use of the notwithstanding clause was appropriate, and whether there are limits to its use.

On Friday, the top court confirmed the validity of Bill 21, but ruled that the law infringes on democratic rights by banning Quebec's elected officials from wearing a face covering for religious reasons.

The court also ruled that a Canadian court has the power to declare whether a law is consistent with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms even if the notwithstanding clause is invoked, but that they would not do so in this case.
While the majority of the seven justices found that Quebec's law is largely valid, some dissented to parts of the decision.

Justices Andromache Karakatsanis, Michelle O'Bonsawin and Nicholas Kasirer wrote that the notwithstanding clause "cannot be used to authorize laws that are incompatible with the fundamental character of Canada as a free and democratic country".
Specifically, they said they believe the law infringes on the charter's guarantee to freedom of religion, freedom of expression and the right to equality.
What to know about the Supreme Court decision on Quebec's secularism bill

Civil liberty groups in Quebec have criticised Bill 21, saying it disproportionately affects Muslim women who wear the hijab, arguing that it has excluded them from key areas of public life in the province.
Stephen Brown, CEO of the National Council of Canadian Muslims, called the law "discriminatory" and criticised the court's decision.
"Entire categories of people are now barred from entire sectors of employment, not because of what they have done, but because of who they are," he said.
The chair of the English Montreal School Board, one of the main groups challenging the law, said the board was "obviously very disappointed" with the ruling.
"It wasn't the result we were looking for," Ortona told reporters. "But we do take solace from a lot of the declarations that were made by the court."
Quebec has argued that the law is necessary to uphold the province's state secularism - or laïcité - as a core component of its identity.

Earlier this year, the province passed another bill expanding its secularism rules to subsidised daycares and post-secondary institutions. It also restricted public prayer with fines for non-compliance.
The leader of the Bloc Québécois, a federal party that advocates for Quebec sovereignty, said Friday's ruling upheld the province's right to protect its values.

"We are now more than ever in a position to move forward with the preservation of the very elements that profoundly define the distinct nature of Quebec society," Yves-François Blanchet told reporters in French.

A court in Kenya has convicted the leader of a doomsday Christian cult of the manslaughter of 123 of his followers.
Paul Mackenzie was found guilty in Mombasa of ordering his followers, all adults, to fast to death in Shakahola forest near the coast between January 2021 and September 2023.
Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for murdering 191 people, all but one of them children, in the same mass killing.
Mackenzie had pleaded not guilty to manslaughter and one of his lawyers said he would appeal against the conviction after sentencing, Reuters news agency reports.

The court also convicted 29 others including Mackenzie's wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, of their part in the manslaughter.
Sixty defendants were acquitted. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated that an appeal would be launched against their acquittal.
The self-styled pastor was arrested in 2023 after the discovery of more than 400 bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest, near the Indian Ocean coast.

The court found Mackenzie had "systematically persuaded his followers to fast until they died", Kenya's Office of The Director of Public Prosecutions said in a statement on Friday's verdict, which it described as "the final conviction" in the cases against him.
"Children were to go first, then women and then men, with Mackenzie himself meant to die last," the office said.
The prosecution argued that Mackenzie and his accomplices had acted together as part of a suicide pact to fast to death in order to "meet Jesus".
Witnesses testified that he had preached that education, medicine and ornaments were sinful.
Those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death, according to the verdict in his trial for the murder of 191 people.
The defendants had claimed that the victims had fasted out of their own free will.

Mackenzie established Good News International Ministries in 2003. Over the next 16 years, the church grew in popularity to draw thousands of followers in branches across Kenya.
A television station called Times TV would broadcast his sermons from his church in the resort town of Malindi.
His End Days sermons included conspiracy theories that described education as "evil", healthcare as "against the doctrine" and digital identity cards as "the mark of the devil".
After the main church shut down in 2019, Mackenzie moved to Shakahola forest, encouraging his devotees to follow him.
The community was described as mud houses scattered across the vast forest.
"We lived a quiet normal life, fasting for a few days then having a small meal," said survivor Peter Shukrani, who was rescued after falling ill.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw07: Millions of women and girls remain unprotected in South Asia because of inadequate laws to deal with marital rape

Failure to fully criminalise marital rape leaves millions of women and girls unprotected in eight South Asian countries, where intimate partner violence is 35% higher than the global average, says a new study.
More than 100 countries have outlawed marital rape, but a large part of South Asia - India, Afghanistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh - remain among the three dozen countries which haven't.
The only South Asian country where rape within marriage attracts the same penalty as any other rape is The Maldives.
Nepal and Bhutan have criminalised marital rape, but apply lesser penalties, says the study by Samaj, a coalition of women's rights groups in the region.
India is among the three dozen countries where marital rape is still not outlawed
South Asia's marital rape laws largely stem from British colonial rule, says Ranjeeta Silwal of Equality Now, a global women's rights group part of Samaj.
The law, dating to 1860 in India and Bangladesh and 1885 in Sri Lanka, lists exceptions to rape - including sex by a man with his adult wife.
Campaigners say the law is outdated and forced sex is rape, regardless of the perpetrator. Experts warn marital sexual violence harms women's physical, psychological, emotional and sexual well-being.
More than 100 countries have criminalised marital rape, including the UK, which changed its law in 1991. But the exemption remains in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.
In India, growing clamour to criminalise rape within marriage
India government says criminalising marital rape 'excessively harsh'

Pakistan removed the marital rape exception in 2006, but no higher court has confirmed that rape laws apply within marriage. A recent high court ruling, meanwhile, granted husbands broad immunity for non-consensual sex.
Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have steadily dismantled women's protections in Afghanistan.

A new penal code introduced in January made matters worse, Silwal says. Under it, a husband can be prosecuted for violence against his wife only if he causes a broken bone, open wound or severe bruising. Even then, he faces just 15 days in prison if convicted.
Unsurprisingly, the code makes no mention of marital rape. But its narrow definition of punishable violence effectively denies women protection against it.
Intimate partner violence is much higher than the global average in South Asian countries
"The idea comes from the belief that consent for sex is implied in marriage, that marriage is a threshold where consent ends," Silwal told the BBC.
"But it shows a lack of awareness, it shows we are still treating women as property, that we are still very patriarchal."
The report comes amid renewed debate over marital rape across the region.
In India, 10 petitions challenging the law are pending before the Supreme Court, which is due to begin final hearings on 9 December.
Courts have delivered contradictory rulings over the years, with some judges acknowledging the law's archaic nature and urging parliament to criminalise marital rape.
There was outrage last year when a court let go a man whose wife had died after he brutally raped her.
But the Indian government, religious organisations and men's rights activists have opposed petitions in the top court, saying criminalisation of marital rape would be " excessively harsh ".
India refuses to criminalise marital rape. This new series shines a light on it
India anger as judge frees man accused of raping wife who then died

Rights groups in Bangladesh have also challenged the marital rape exception, arguing it violates constitutional rights to life, liberty and protection from torture and cruel treatment, the report says.

A study of 40,000 people over three decades found Britons are having less sex, and local experts have thoughts on why the same is happening here.
A big new British study has revealed a sex slump, especially among young adults, and local experts reckon the same can be said about New Zealanders.
A third of people aged between 16 and 24 in Britain say they've never had sex, according to a the UK National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles .
The study tracked the sexual behaviour of nearly 40,000 people in Britain over more than three decades.
Sexual frequency among adults under 45 almost halved in the past 30 years, it found.
Young people are less likely to get hot and heavy these days, the survey found.
On average, couples say between one and three times a week feels good for them, but frequency isn't the only measure of a good sex life, experts say.
Many parents – fathers in particular – find even the idea of these conversations mortifying.
Gen Z's lack of interest in sex has been shaped by the #MeToo movement, skewed self-perception and exposure to pornography at a very young age, says neuroscientist Dr Debra Soh.

While New Zealand data on the frequency of sex is limited, experts say we are much the same.

Sexual experiences for New Zealand youth had been on a downward slope for the entire 21st century, according to a series of surveys done on high schoolers throughout the 2000s by the Ministry of Social Development and other agencies.
Between 2001 and 2019, high schoolers having sexual experiences lowered by about 10 percent down to just 20 percent, according to the formally long-running Youth2000 survey.
Last year, 15.7 percent of those aged 13 to 19 claimed to be having consensual sex, according to a similar survey called Youth Health and Wellbeing Survey 2025 .
Sex therapist Jo Robertson said the decrease could be linked to online sexual activity and a lack of social interaction.

"Online doesn't demand anything from you, does it? Whether it's an AI companion or whether it's porn, it's not asking you to do anything. It's not asking you to be kind. It's not asking you to ask them on a date."

“For the longest time, I was hoping and expecting it to happen organically and now it feels like intervention is required.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6r7: There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.
Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.
"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.
Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the US is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.
US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC , external : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."
The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.
It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: Nessar Khawaja told almost 70,000 social media followers his network makes money from "desperate" customers
Organised networks of rogue plumbers and electricians have been scamming people on a large scale, a BBC investigation has found.

Clive said the engineer spent about two hours at the property before presenting him with the bill.
He added he had felt pressured into paying as the work had already been completed.
He went to his local bank branch to move money between accounts before returning home and making the payment through the engineer's portable card reader.
Despite his doubts about the costs, Clive said he had feared what might happen if he refused to pay.
"If I hadn't paid him, I thought something might happen," he said.

Sky-high bills. Hostile threats. What happens when the person you hire to fix a domestic problem is plotting to rip you off?
While the BBC has not seen evidence that Khawaja controls or runs this company, it has established the following:
Companies House places Chriss Electrician Ltd at an address in Ilford
Khawaja appears as the listed director of two dissolved companies inside that same building, one inside the very same flat

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck20: The UK has agreed the deals in a bid to cut red tape for British companies
The UK will pay a "participation fee" to the EU as part of the deals agreed by Andy Burnham, according to legal documents.
The surcharge will go towards the running costs of EU agencies and systems required to deliver two of the agreements unveiled by the prime minister last week.
It will be paid in addition to a contribution towards costs that broadly mirrors how EU members contribute to the bloc's shared budget, the documents show.

The government has sought to contrast the financial costs of the deals against their overall effect on the economy, which it estimates will receive an eventual boost by billions a year due to increased trade.

The government is yet to publish an estimate of overall additional costs, but officials said they expected them to be in the low tens of millions per year and "massively outweighed" by predicted economic gains.

British ministers had already said they were prepared to pay towards administrative costs required to implement deals to re-link the UK to the EU's carbon trading regime, and align Britain with the EU's food standards.
Now, details of how the payments will be calculated have been revealed in treaties to deliver the two agreements, which are meant to take effect during 2028.
Legal text for a third agreement agreed last week, on youth visas for 18 to 31 year olds, is expected to be published in the coming days.

According to the treaties, the payments will be made as a share of the running costs of three EU agencies, as well as various systems that will be used to implement the food standards and emissions deals.
The bulk of the payments, to be made in euros, will come in the form of an "operational contribution" in proportion to the size of the British economy compared to that of the EU.
This broadly mirrors the way in which EU member states split the cost of their main contributions towards the bloc's overall budget.
But in addition, the UK will also pay a "participation fee" set at 4% of its main contribution figure.

The government has pointed to the 2021 Brexit trade agreement negotiated by the Conservatives, which also applied an additional surcharge to UK contributions towards the cost of relevant EU programmes.
However, any additional contributions are likely to be seized upon by opponents of the latest deals.

Ministers had declined to enter into specifics of the fees during negotiations on the treaties. On Sunday, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the latest deals agreed by Burnham were "not about cost to the taxpayer".
It comes as the government published separate legislation granting it broad powers to incorporate new EU laws required to implement the agreements, without having to hold a full vote each time.
The food standards deal in particular will mean Britain will have to align with scores of current EU food-related laws that have been updated since Brexit, along with future rules in these areas.
The government argues the new powers are required because it would be impractical to run a full parliamentary process each time UK legislation needs to be updated to make the agreement work.
But it has prompted criticism from opposition parties, because the UK no longer has voting rights at the EU to shape European legislation.

The government argues the UK will get a say on new rules, with the treaty texts confirming British experts can be consulted when new EU laws are being drawn up, with the UK granted "observer" status in certain meetings.
But Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham was showing "disdain for the democratic process" by asking for a "blank cheque to install and enact EU law".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqev: Trump boosts Nvidia boss return but are US politicians on board?
Jensen Huang's extraordinary return as Nvidia's boss rocked not only its shares in New York but also sent shockwaves through the artificial intelligence (AI) industry around the world.
Those jolts were felt particularly in Asia as the saga highlighted the region's huge exposure to the technology.

Tech-heavy stock indexes in Japan, South Korea and Taiwan went on a rollercoaster ride this week. Markets soared after a near-trillion dollar surge in Nvidia's share price but then slumped as concerns about political and regulatory scrutiny hit investor confidence.

The chipmaker is a "symbolic bellwether" of the AI trade that is fast becoming key to places like South Korea, Taiwan, Singapore and Malaysia," says Dylan Loh, an international studies lecturer at Nanyang Technological University.
From chip manufacturing to data centres to foreign investments, AI has become a strategic priority for these economies - and they are now increasingly dependent on Nvidia's fortunes.
In Nvidia, the AI industry has the unrivalled power of cutting-edge chips and the financial clout that turned it into "the bank of AI". And in Huang, it has a high-profile evangelist.
That combination has put it at the heart of the AI ecosystem in more ways than one.
For one, Nvidia was able to grow rapidly by outsourcing chip production instead of having to spend heavily to build its own manufacturing plants.
It contracts out most of its production to Taiwanese chipmaking giant TSMC.
That means Taiwan is vulnerable to changes in AI tech demand, says Paul Cavey, founder of Taipei-based research firm East Asia Econ.
"The surge in [Taiwan's] real economic growth since 2024 has been because of the big increase in AI related exports".
Huang said earlier this year that Nvidia plans to invest around $150bn (£114.4bn) a year in Taiwan at a launch to celebrate the firm's planned headquarters on the island.

To a lesser extent, South Korea and Japan are also exposed to the industry, Cavey adds. They are among its suppliers of key components such as memory chips and testing equipment, with firms like Samsung and SK Hynix making the firm's processors.
On top of that, Nvidia is a financial backstop and major lender to companies in the AI supply chain.
Data centres worth billions of dollars are being built in Malaysia

It is difficult to overstate the role Nvidia, with Huang at its helm, has played in the region's AI industry. Nvidia's chips fill its data centres, power its AI models and feed the companies making cars and electronics.
"Asia isn't just a customer base for Nvidia. It is an indispensable engine of the company's AI dominance because of East Asia's semiconductor manufacturing and memory ecosystems," Loh says.

In the Asia-Pacific region, the data centre market, which is largely powered by Nvidia chips, is in the midst of an "unprecedented boom", according to property services firm CBRE , external . The volume of investment has been rising steadily in recent years to reach a record of $11.6bn (£8.85bn) in 2025.

In South East Asia, Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed had become the region's biggest buyer of Nvidia chips before it was accused of smuggling them to China. Megaspeed has said it "conducts legitimate and lawful business" and has "retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation".
The US has said it intends to ban Megaspeed Ltd from doing business in the United States.
But in a timely example of the importance of AI to this region, Singapore this week further raised its growth forecast for this year as the technology boosts its economy.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8d: Self-confessed foodie Catherine has booked tables for one in the UK and abroad

Catherine Smith is perusing the menu at a high-end Mediterranean restaurant she has been excited to try. She has a new outfit on, and as she sips her rosé, she looks across at the empty seat opposite - bliss.
"I think what is so special about solo dining is that you don't have to wait for people to make those plans. You can go out and do them yourself," says the 23-year-old.
The self-confessed foodie is part of a growing trend of people booking tables for one - not because they're away with work but as a treat.
As food trends analyst Charles Banks puts it: "[Eating alone] is becoming an intentional act, a little pocket of independence, indulgence and self-care."
We spoke to solo dining fans and hospitality industry experts about how the trend is shaping the restaurant experience and asked if you would book a table for one.
Catherine, from Yorkshire, began dining solo at university and now does it at least once a month, choosing high-end restaurants she would not usually go to with friends and family.
She has been to a range of places both in the UK and abroad, doing "lots of research" to find new spots, typically spending £100 to £200 per meal.
"I think because a lot of my friends are vegan or vegetarian, I find that difficult sometimes because I'm quite a big meat eater," she says.
"I find it nice to be able to go out and pick a restaurant where I haven't had to scour through the menu to make sure that it's suitable for them."
Catherine says the sense of freedom she gets from picking where and when she eats "feels empowering".
"It definitely feels like not only a form of self-care but also a form of female liberation."
While solo dining Catherine likes to read, journal or simply enjoy the peace and quiet

Online booking platform OpenTable says it covers more than 5,000 restaurants in the UK. It says solo dining makes up the smallest proportion of its bookings in the UK but it is the fastest-growing category.
Figures from 1 January to 31 August this year saw a rise of 23% in solo bookings compared to the same time period a year ago. It did not provide the data to the BBC to verify.
Nishi Singh was an avid solo diner when she lived in London, but found it wasn't widely accepted after moving to Delhi.
"Someone approached me and said that they assumed I'd been stood up," she tells BBC World Service's The Food Chain podcast.
"It sparked a conversation about the culture around solo dining in Delhi and I was really shocked to hear that it's not really something people do."
A couple of days later, she started documenting her solo dining experience on social media.
"Quite a lot of people have reached out and said that this is something they'd like to do and they're too scared to do it themselves," she says.

Banks, joint managing director of The Food People, a food trends and ideas agency, says that while solo dining isn't a "new consumer behaviour", changes in society mean it has become "almost aspirational".
But he notes that not every restaurant has welcomed the trend.
"A single diner could therefore feel like an inefficient use of a table rather than a customer the restaurant actively wanted."
Yousaf thinks solo diners could produce another useful business stream for restaurants
SoloTable, a website that helps identify restaurants suitable for solo diners, found that one in eight of 178 restaurants it surveyed in London did not accept online reservations from solo diners.

Catherine says she has previously been turned away. "There are a lot of restaurants that I've wanted to go to before where they don't actually allow solo diners. And I've always found that to be really disappointing."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c52e: Jim Lembesis has been working on elevators in Chicago for 47 years
Some of them are angry. Nerves are frayed. Many of them are just relieved that he's here.

When a lift stops working in Chicago, frazzled building managers might get a visit from Jim Lembesis. For more than 47 years, Lembesis has repaired and upgraded lifts. He says he understands why staff and residents are so anxious to have things working again.
"They wait and they wait," says Lembesis, a field technician for Parkway Elevators. "There's a lot of frustration. Sometimes it's a repeat issue. It's a never-ending cycle, you know what I mean?"

The widely reported shortage of lift and escalator mechanics in the US, which is also a problem in many other countries, has got worse over time, he adds: "It's been like night and day compared to when I started."
Lift and escalator technicians "amaze" with their ability to fix things
Everyone needs a lift now and again. Some people depend on them – elderly residents of high-rise buildings, say, or wheelchair users.

Storm-damaged lifts in Hawaiian apartment blocks this year left some residents trapped , external in their homes for weeks. A lack of mechanics, and problems sourcing parts, were blamed for the repair delays.
In the US, the average salary for a lift mechanic , external is $110,000 (£83,000). And yet people in the industry say it is difficult to attract new workers.

Sure, says Lembesis, you do encounter some dangers in a job like this. There are risks of falling from a great height – or being electrocuted. Once, he was even hit on the head with an umbrella by an elderly lady after he rescued her from a stuck lift.

But there are so many skills to learn, and great camaraderie and knowledge-sharing among mechanics, he says. As one recruiter puts it, these technicians amaze people with their ability to fix things. They are like "wizards". The overall-clad shamans who know how to get modern life running again.

Nine times out of 10, the problem is with the doors, says Lembesis. These components repeatedly move back and forth. "People hit them with carts, and dirt and debris [falls into them]," says Lembesis. "[The doors] take the most beating."
Mechanics often keep various spare door parts in their vehicles, ready to use.

But technicians like Lembesis don't just have to get lifts working, they also have to verify the lifts are safe. He remembers one case, decades ago, getting called out to a burning building. His role was to ensure the lifts, which were being drenched with huge volumes of water, were still safe to use while firefighters tackled the blaze.
"I was there for 15 hours that night," he says. "Everyone, on the way out of the door, shook my hand."
In the US there's a four-year apprenticeship to become a lift technician

Finding good lift technicians is "becoming more difficult" says Matt Hollinshead, president of the US National Association for Elevator Contractors. "We have a four-year apprenticeship," he says. That's the first hurdle. And many states require certification or licensing before you can work on lifts.
"We have a vast array of equipment that has to be maintained in the United States." Some lifts are 100-years-old. As time goes on, the technological knowledge required to repair them only grows.

Hollinshead says that weeks or months-long delays to lift repairs are not typically due to staff shortages but that, in such cases, it's likely that a particular part isn't readily available. Manufacturing a replacement hydraulic cylinder takes six to 12 weeks, he notes.
But the lack of technicians does mean that that building managers might have to wait days before someone can even diagnose what's wrong with a lift after it stops working.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62k: The number one target is US-based Gordon Brothers who bought the discount chain for £1 and have taken nearly £20m out of the business already.

The team running Poundland blame the owners for strangling their ability to turn the business around, saying that their access to Poundland's own cash was restricted, leaving them unable to fully restock ahead of the crucial Christmas period.

Martin Property Group offered £5m up front with the balance to be deferred, while Xyra Holdings offered £12.5m up front but, according to sources close to the deal, were thought unable to actually pay.
Unsurprisingly perhaps, Gordon Brothers dispute a lot of how they have been characterised.
First, they insist that they lent the business £85m to try to keep it alive for the 17 months since they bought it. Without them, this collapse would have happened in June last year.
The £20m taken out of the business since then has mostly been interest on that loan.

Despite brief periods of sales growth compared with a year earlier, Poundland was not generating enough cash to sustain itself. Sales were forecast to be £115m lower than predicted when Gordon Brothers bought the business - more than offsetting a £100m cost-cutting programme.
Like other retailers Poundland was hit by rising labour costs, employment taxes and business rates.
In the end, argue Gordon Brothers, none of the potential buyers could meet their terms and prove they had the money and expertise to make a go of it.
Such is the discrepancy between the two versions that the chair of the Business Committee wants Gordon Brothers and the management back in front of them to get to the truth.
It is still possible that a bidder may emerge in the coming hours and days to save the business as a whole but most industry observers think that looks unlikely.

Julie Palmer of insolvency specialists Begbies Traynor told the BBC: "This sort of direction of travel seemed somehow inevitable. Obviously, if one of those interested parties steps up and buys the whole business and assets, that's the best, quickest and cleanest outcome. I think realistically, though, there is a chance now that there will be a breakup."
Like previous busts such as Woolworths, BHS and Wilko, many of these stores will find new owners and they will need local, experienced staff.
But none of that will be much comfort to those workers facing grave uncertainty a month before Christmas, when they should be at their busiest and most needed.
Gordon Brothers specialise in situations of commercial distress. When they take on a distressed company, they try to make sure that the worst possible outcome is still one that makes money for them.
In this situation, the worst outcome would mean they get paid back £22.5m, earn interest on the loan they provided the company (secured against the company assets) and a few other miscellaneous fees.

Little wonder then that many people say they had little incentive to strain every sinew to secure a buyer. They argue they kept a business that would have collapsed last June going for another 17 months, which extended employment for thousands of workers.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg5: More people face higher mortgage repayments when they roll off a fixed deal than previously estimated, new figures from the the Bank of England show.

She is far from alone, with one million homeowners facing a similar increase often because they are coming off deals that were agreed before interest rates began rising in 2022.
The Bank's report said that households facing higher payments "may need to reduce discretionary spending or draw down savings as higher energy and other essential costs feed through".
Most had savings buffers but lower-income households, including renters, had less wriggle room owing to spending a greater proportion of their income on essentials.
Early in November, the Bank raised the benchmark interest rate , which influences borrowing costs for individuals and businesses, for the first time in more than three years, from 3.75% to 4%.
The numbers could change were mortgage rates to fall, primarily if international economic volatility eased.
Even so, the Bank said around 350,000 were already projected to see monthly mortgage repayments fall when they fixed their next deal within three years.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6z9: Poundland has collapsed into administration, leaving the jobs of its 11,000 staff in doubt in the run-up to Christmas.
The company has appointed consultancy Alix Partners to oversee a sale of part or all of the discount retailer, with questions remaining about the future of the company.
Poundland shops will remain open as usual for now. The firm collapsing has acted as a reset in the process of selling it.
Administrators are looking to either sell the business as a whole, or to break it up, which is the more likely outcome.

When Poundland was still a going concern, Irish property firm Martin Property Group made an offer for it. But a source said the group was now "unlikely" to make a fresh bid due to "irreparable harm" to the brand from the administration process.
Before the collapse, Fortress, which owns rival budget chain Poundstretcher, was interested in buying about 200 of the stores, and wanted to keep those trading under the Poundland brand.
But Fortress's position at the moment is unclear. The BBC understands it is considering selling Poundstretcher, a move first reported by Bloomberg.
A decision on Poundstretcher could come before the end of this week. However, Fortress has declined to comment.
When the chain was sold by Pepco last year for £1 it was struggling. It suffered a £68m loss that year.
Poundland's managing director Barry Williams said Poundland had been seeing a "strong recovery" and recorded a profit by one measure in the first nine months of this year.

Poundland's management paint a picture of a retailer that was turning a corner until the owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, pulled the plug on funding for day-to-day expenses such as buying stock.
The Usdaw union, which represents shopworkers, claim the owners forced Poundland into administration.

Labour MP Antonia Bance said she was "pretty appalled" by the conduct of Gordon Brothers over the past few weeks, and that it was going to make much bigger profits by breaking up the business rather than by keeping it going.
However, Gordon Brothers insisted the business was only turning a profit on paper, and had missed budget forecasts.
A spokeswoman said while the management team had made £100m in cost reductions, the business had moved from a £70m loss to "around break-even".
"Break-even is different from generating the cash needed to buy stock, invest, and withstand increasing economic pressures," the spokeswoman said. "A few good weeks do not make a turnaround."
Poundland repeatedly missed budget targets over the year, the spokeswoman added.
Gordon Brothers was concerned that as inflation goes up next year, those pressures would have helped to make the business unviable, it said.

And Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency agency Begbies Traynor, said Poundland's collapse "seemed somehow inevitable" due to challenges facing retailers - including higher costs to employ staff.
Stores are still trading while the administrators work out if the business is viable.
The funds locked up by Gordon Brothers - at the last count about £70m - have now been released by the administrators.
This has turned the taps back on, so staff will continue to be paid in the run-up to Christmas, and so will suppliers.

But here's the catch: the administrators have a legal obligation to maximise value for "secured" creditors. It means the owners, Gordon Brothers, are at the head of the queue for being paid back the loans that were stumbling blocks in the negotiations.

But more importantly for staff, if the administrators can get more value by breaking up the business than by selling it as a whole, then that is what they have to do, even if the business would be viable.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9kg: The Norwegian low cost carrier Norse Atlantic Airways has suspended all flights as it rushes to resolve what it warned is a critical financial situation.
The airline said if no solution can be found, it intends to file for bankruptcy.
It uses a fleet of 12 Boeing 787 aircraft on long-haul routes from a number of European airports, including London Gatwick, Rome and Oslo.
Prior to the suspension of flights, it was advertising services from London to Orlando, Cape Town, Bangkok and Phuket.
One aircraft was meant to depart London for Orlando this morning, while another was meant to arrive from Cape Town this evening.
The suspension has also affected Pakistan International Airlines, which had been leasing aircraft and crews from Norse Atlantic.
PIA was forced to cancel services from London to Islamabad and from Manchester to Lahore last night.
In a statement on social media, PIA said all UK flights from today would be operated by aircraft from its own fleet.
Londoner Fred was due to fly to Cape Town with Norse Atlantic next week for a friend's wedding, but has decided to change his plans.
"Yesterday the exact same flight I was going to get was cancelled, so I was worried" he told the BBC's Your Voice. "I sent an email to Norse and have had nothing back".
He decided to rebook with a different airline, which cost him an extra £1,000.
Another traveller, Claire from Herefordshire, is currently on holiday in South Africa with her daughter.
"We are due to fly home on Sunday and are now looking at a really expensive flight back," she said.
"We have tried contacting Norse but have been given an automated response saying someone will get back to us within three business days."
Consumer group Which? advised Norse Atlantic customers to not cancel their flights as the airline has not collapsed. Doing so removes passengers' right to a refund.

Rory Boland, Which? travel editor, said: "If Norse does go bust, whether you get a refund depends on how you booked and paid. If you booked directly with Norse, you may be able to claim a refund via your credit card provider, or possibly your debit card."
Those stuck abroad should contact insurers, while those with package holidays reliant on Norse Atlantic flights should contact their tour operator, he added.
Norse Atlantic Airways was set up in 2021 as a low-cost long-haul carrier.
It entered the market as a successor to Norwegian, which withdrew from long haul routes as a result of the Covid pandemic.
But it has struggled to make money, and its problems worsened this year, as fuel prices rocketed due to the war in Iran.
Unlike many other European carriers, Norse Atlantic does not hedge its fuel bills by buying supplies in advance at fixed prices.
This left it fully exposed when prices soared, with the cost of fuel roughly doubling at one point. Prices remain significantly higher than they were before the conflict began.
In the first half of the year Norse Atlantic made a loss of $94.6m.
In a statement to the Oslo Stock Exchange on Wednesday, the airline said its financial situation was critical, and it needed to find short term funding to continue its operations.
After suspending flights, the company said it was in discussions with investors regarding a possible takeover that "would include a financing solution".
However, it said if short term funding could not be found quickly, "it is the Board's intention to file for bankruptcy".

Its potential collapse follows the failure of Spirit Airlines in May . The US-based low cost carrier was another airline left exposed when jet fuel prices soared, as US airlines typically do not hedge their purchases.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjql: Over-70s will have to take eye tests every three years or face losing their driving licence under new road safety plans.
Mandatory eyesight tests are part of the Department for Transport's (DfT) road safety strategy, expected within weeks.
Around 6.5 million over-70s hold drivers' licences, with 1.6 million of those aged 80 or over.
To drive legally in the UK, you must be able to read a standard number plate from 20 metres away, wearing glasses or contact lenses if required.

Government sources told the BBC ministers will recommend over-70s be made to regularly prove their eyesight meets the minimum standards. Those who do not, or who fail to meet the minimum standard face losing their licence.
The change follows a consultation which launched early last year , set to recommend a shake-up of the rules for older drivers.
Under the current rules, over 70s have to renew their licence every three years, but only have to self-certify that their sight.

Dennis Reed, of campaign group Silver Voices, which represents older people, said it was "discriminatory to just pick an age out of the hat and say 'everybody over 70 has to go through this, but nobody else does'".
But he said the group is not opposed in principle to regular eye tests for older drivers.
The changes being considered were first reported by the Daily Mail , external .
The NHS provides free eye tests for over 60s, but they are not detailed enough to approve someone to drive.
The BBC understands this system is also being looked at, with the free tests likely to be expanded to become more rigorous.
A Government source said "beefed up measures" were long overdue.
"One life lost on the roads is one too many," they added. "There have been several arguably preventable fatalities on Britain's roads caused by drivers with failing eyesight in recent years.
The DfT said no decision has officially been made on mandating eyesight tests for drivers aged 70 and over.
A spokesperson said: "We recognise the importance of driving for older people's independence but need to balance this with our priority to keep everyone safe on our roads and avoid tragic accidents.
"Mandatory eye tests for drivers over 70 as part of our Road Safety Strategy are one way to do this.
"We are carefully reviewing consultation results," they added. "Older drivers who are fit to drive and have good enough vision have nothing to worry about."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r: The government and the EU have published the texts of two treaties agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.
The treaties were published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The deal covering food exports has a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay "reasonable and proportionate costs" to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.
Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would scrap the deal while Reform UK's Nigel Farage has suggested he would refuse to pay.
The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the future of the UK-EU relationship.
The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
Two of the three legal texts were released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.
A new assessment of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country was also released.
Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students
Farage helps launch new campaign against the UK rejoining the EU

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost the export of major agricultural commodities.
The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."
A plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text also contains finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules. The UK will be invited to attend European Commission meetings and expert groups as an observer, as well as taking part in emergency food security planning.
Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, are detailed in the legislation.
Such powers will enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.
Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".
Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.
Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.
Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".
