https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c2l9: Millions of drivers who were mis-sold car finance agreements could face further delays to compensation after the financial regulator said it had made some errors in its calculations.
Driver have already been told they must wait until at least 2027 to receive compensation, although some may be offered an early settlement.
Average payments of about £829 are expected under the rules published by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA).
However, legal challenges to the scheme - which will be heard in February 2027 -mean compensation calculations and payments have been delayed.
The vast majority of new cars, and many second-hand ones, are bought with finance agreements. Customers pay an initial deposit to secure the vehicle, then a monthly fee with interest.
Compensation could be given to many of those who took out a car loan between April 2007 and November 2024.
The decision by the FCA, the financial regulator, applies to about 12 million car loans - about 37% of the total number during the period.

In 2021, the FCA banned deals where car dealers received commission from lenders, based on the interest rate charged to the customer. These were known as discretionary commission arrangements (DCAs) and customers were often not told about them.
The FCA said this provided an incentive for a buyer to be charged a higher-than-necessary interest rate, leaving them paying too much.
Other car buyers were also judged to have signed unfair contracts because the commission paid to the dealer was so high - accounting for 39% of the total cost of credit and 10% of the loan.
Some customers were not given accurate information about the best finance deal because of exclusive arrangements between car dealers and lenders.
Under the latest proposals, the FCA expects average payouts of £829 per mis-sold agreement.
The total cost of the compensation, including administrative costs, could hit £9.1bn.
How much individual consumers receive will depend on the degree of harm suffered.
The FCA has announced some claimants might be offered an early settlement, but only if it as good as what would be paid under the current proposed central scheme.
Complaints have already been made about four million finance agreements. Those people do not need to do anything.
The regulator urged anyone who has not yet complained to contact their car loan provider directly, rather than using a third-party claims management company.
The regulator's central compensation scheme allows people to complain and potentially receive compensation for mis-sold deals without the need for a lawyer or to go through the courts.
Motorists have also been warned to be on the alert for scammers posing as car finance lenders offering fake compensation .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3v: Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.
Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.
Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.
"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.

Bally Auluk, national officer at the union Usdaw, which represents Poundland workers, told the BBC'S Wake Up to Money programme that Gordon Brothers' "intention was perfectly clear from the offset... to force the company into administration".
"It's such a devastating blow any time of year, but most certainly in the run up to Christmas for 11,000 colleagues, most of whom are our members," he said.
Gordon Brothers rejected Auluk's characterisation of the process and said it had "explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company".
Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.
"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.
"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".
He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said protecting staff is the government's top priority.

"I'm also very mindful that for lots of people across the country, Poundland is a place they go on the high street to get bargains and... given the cost of living challenges we face, that is of concern to us in government," he told the BBC.
Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said it would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".
"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.
Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.
On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.
But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm1w: The government has not confirmed what triggered the shutdown of DWP services
Online benefits and pensions services were still down on Saturday morning following a "cyber incident" which forced the government to take them offline.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has not specified what triggered it to shut down access late on Thursday but has not ruled out that it was hit by hackers.

The government has assured benefits recipients and pensioners that usual payments will continue to be made after some claimants reported delays. It is understood the department believes delays were not linked to the cyber incident.
The UK's former chief technology officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the department had been targeted by hackers.
He continued: "[The government has] taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door."

John Curry, a leading cyber security expert based at Bath Spa University, told BBC News the DWP had "almost certainly" detected hacking activity taking place and shut down its systems in an effort to stop data being stolen.
Curry said if the DWP had discovered hackers inside its computer systems, then the "best thing to do is slam the front door shut".

He also said the government may deliberately release limited information in order to "keep the enemy in the dark" and not give any possible hackers hints about ongoing work to secure sensitive systems.

On Friday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there had been a "serious cyber incident" without offering further details, while the department said the move to close online services was a "precaution".
Downing Street would not be drawn on whether the DWP had been targeted by hackers but did say other departments had not been accessed by a "malicious actor".
The government said it was working with GCHQ's National Cyber Security Centre to investigate the incident, which indicates a hack has not been ruled out.

The incident has fuelled concerns about the vulnerability of state computer systems and whether security protocols are keeping pace with demand and advances in AI technology, which can be used to aid hackers.

Matthew Gould, former Cabinet Office head of cyber security, said: "There are hundreds and hundreds of legacy systems that are kept going with huge commitment and skill from the people doing it, but where frankly the system is relying on very old infrastructure."
He added: "What is needed a lot of the time is quite boring investment in upgrading what is already there, moving platforms on to more stable bases, making systems more resilient.
"It doesn't make for great headlines but there is an awful lot of investment that's required on a digital estate as large as the government's or the NHS's to keep it strong and resilient."
DWP said it took some online services offline as a precaution
The DWP makes around 2.5 million payments every day and is the primary source of income for millions of people.
Some benefits claimants have reported delays in receiving their money and said they fear being penalised for not submitting information to the DWP on time.
Jacob Dwight, 21, from Stockport, is concerned he could lose quarter of his income as he has been unable to access his Universal Credit account to explain why he missed a meeting.
Dwight, a design graduate, said he would not be able to buy any Christmas presents if his claim was fully voided.
"More importantly, UC is essentially paying my heating bill at the moment," he added.
Benyamin Abdollahi, 19, a part-time university student and full-time carer for his mother, said he was facing financial worries this weekend.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c64g: Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem – and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.
Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.
The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch – 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.
This time it may not have that luxury – in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.
These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.
Grand Theft Auto 6 saw record retail sales in its first full day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history
Barely a week after the release of GTA 6, efforts are already under way to get an unofficial version playable on PC, although some projects have faced takedown notices from the game's publisher.
For some gamers, it's an exciting prospect, despite the legal questions surrounding the process.
For developers, it may be a warning: if a game as big as GTA 6 can be recreated, what does that mean for everyone else?
The recent wave of AI-assisted game recreation has been widely linked to Anthropic's Opus 5.5 model, released in September, and to agentic tools such as Claude Code.
Mark Brown, creator of the YouTube channel Game Maker's Toolkit whose own game Word Play was recently recreated using AI, said cloning largely took two forms: replication and reverse engineering.
Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one, possibly using screenshots or a description.
This, he said, was similar to "looking at a painting and making your own replica" – something which is "a very close copy, but is ultimately a new painting".
It's a particular issue among smaller studios, many of whom worry that AI makes it easier for others to copy their work.

When indie developers Sodoj and Marco from the studio Robotonic noticed a version of their unreleased puzzle game 204Snake appear on the free games platform Yandex with the same name, they were "appalled".
"The game was essentially the exact same idea, the exact same mechanics as we had, but with the art looking a bit off," Marco told the BBC .
Replication is where someone asks an AI chatbot such as Claude or ChatGPT to build a new game based on an existing one
The second approach – reverse engineering – involves working backwards from a finished game to understand how it was created.
One way of doing this is decompilation, which attempts to turn the game's final version into something closer to its original source code.
Brown compares the process to "taking a cake and somehow turning it back into the original recipe, with the exact quantities of flour, eggs, and milk used, so anyone can remake the same cake".
Reverse-engineering projects have helped bring games such as Halo: Combat Evolved and Grand Theft Auto: Vice City to web browsers.
A related technique, recompilation, can help adapt a game that has been reverse-engineered to run on different hardware. This is one of the methods being explored in efforts to get GTA 6 onto PC.
Coders wanting to attempt this with Rockstar's latest game face a difficult task because of its sheer size and complexity.

Earlier in November, Cyberleek – a hacker or group of hackers – released what they claimed to be a near-complete Xbox development build of the game. They later leaked what they claimed to be the missing .exe file needed to launch the game.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8: SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.
The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, would "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

However, rival firm Amazon has criticised it as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan", while astronomers in the US said the move would "significantly undermine" the public's ability to study and observe the night sky.
There is increasing opposition to data centres on earth, including in the US where experts say they were a factor in the Republicans big losses in the midterm elections.

SpaceX believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".
FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".
"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.
Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."
Did a data centre revolt affect the US midterm election results?
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites must begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.
The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).
Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

Speaking to the Today programme, on BBC Radio 4, Prof Sir Martin Sweeting, founder and executive chairman of Surrey Satellite Technology Ltd, said while the idea of data centres in space seemed "technically feasible", whether it "makes sense at scale yet" still needed to be analysed.
Being able to get the data from the network of satellites, he added, would depend on being able to use laser links from the ground to them.
"That has not yet been perfected to the level at which it would be able to support the huge amounts of data that are likely to be transferred backwards and forwards," he said.
Meanwhile, the American Astronomical Society (AAS) said it was "disheartened and dismayed" by the decision.

It said the proposed constellation would "significantly undermine decades of federal investment in astronomical facilities" as well as "the ability of astronomers and the public to enjoy and study the night sky".

It noted that the constellation "involves larger (and therefore brighter) and more numerous objects", meaning the satellites would "be visible as extremely bright objects for longer periods in the night sky".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmy4: Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial at Brooklyn federal court on November 17.
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.
In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.
Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.
Huawei said , external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".
Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.
However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.
Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.
Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.
"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement , external .
"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."
The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.
Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.
Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.
"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."
Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.
"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: John Motson was a legendary football commentator who covered 10 World Cups, 10 European Championships and 29 FA Cup finals for BBC Sport

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August , told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.
The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.
"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.
"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

WATCH: The new John Motson commentary in EA Sports FC 27 - and how it sounded back in Fifa 1998
John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.
"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.
EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.
"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.
Gazza's tears, Radford's screamer & the Crazy Gang - 5 of Motty's best
Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.
"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3rr: Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?
Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned . Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.
Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.
Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.
There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.
Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.
There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.
For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.
But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.
As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.
"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X , external .
Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.
Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.
Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.
Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.
So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)
Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.
Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.
For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).
Nvidia's clothing lines quickly sell out, bought by fans of the tech giant

In addition, Huang has powerful allies, and they are mostly powerful men. US President Donald Trump personally pushed for his return to Nvidia, while Elon Musk said it would be "an honour" to work with him at SpaceX.
He is one of very few people who knows both Trump and China's President Xi Jinping personally - and somehow he has surfed the geopolitical tension between the two continents.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crpd: US Attorney General Todd Blanche has backed Nvidia as a "good corporate citizen" while refusing to comment on whether the AI chipmaker was under federal investigation.
Blanche said he had no information about newly reinstated CEO Jensen Huang's security clearance status, as lawmakers demand answers about US President Donald Trump's involvement in Huang's comeback.
Huang was given his job back less than two weeks after being forced to resign over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.
Asked several times on Tuesday whether the justice department or FBI had investigated Huang, Blanche responded: "I don't know what you're talking about."

Huang is still set to appear before Congress next week, where he will be questioned about national security concerns over his relationship with an alleged spy who previously ran Megaspeed, a Singapore-based corporate customer of Nvidia.
Trump has said he would consider pardoning Huang for any potential criminal activity, though he does not think it will come to that.
"It's always an option, I guess, but I don't think it'll be necessary," Trump told the New York Post in an interview published on Tuesday.
With Huang rescue, Trump riskily ties his political fortunes to Nvidia
The US commerce department has also announced it was preparing to blacklist the tech company Megaspeed, which has been suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.
The commerce and justice departments said last week that they began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 "for potential export control violations" .
But Blanche told reporters on Tuesday that the latter had "hundreds, if not more" export investigations occurring at any one time.
"So when you say the export investigation is still ongoing, I don't know what you're talking about," he said.

Asked if he was satisfied Nvidia had been co-operative with inquiries into whether it or Huang knew about chips being diverted to China, Blanche said: "I have no reason to stand up here and say Nvidia is anything but a good corporate citizen.

While Nvidia's stock market value surged on the announcement of Huang's reappointment, some of the gains were reversed in volatile Tuesday trading.
The company's share price closed down nearly 6% - still well above where it ended last week. On Monday, Nvidia stock rocketed more than 31% following news of Huang's return.

Huang reportedly apologised to Nvidia employees on Tuesday, the day after returning to the company as chief executive, saying he had made "terrible mistakes" and was now receiving daily 90-minute therapy sessions.
The company's board reinstated Huang on Monday in a shock U-turn. Harvey Jones, its chairman, said Huang's return was in the "best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers".
The board said it had received input from senior levels of the US government and was confident that Huang's reinstatement posed no national security risk.

Republican Congressman Don Bacon said Nvidia should have "ignored the administration's inexplicable desire to save Huang".
Republican Senator Pete Ricketts said Huang's behaviour "doesn't absolve Nvidia of answering for national security concerns and unaccounted-for chips".

Democratic Congressman Robert Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, said Trump's "direct involvement" with Nvidia's decision "raises serious national security and corruption questions".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmwy: Selena Buse, 16, reverses her Citroën Ami out of a parking space and heads off past the school playground. Heads turn. The Ami looks pretty remarkable. Futurist or like-a-toaster depending on your point of view. But it's changed her life.
"I got it because I really needed it to get to school. And I use it to visit friends on the weekends. It's indispensable in rural areas like where I live," she says.
In France, you can drive a car like this from the age of 14 with a road safety certificate and eight hours training. In Italy too.
In Germany and Spain it's 15, in the UK 16 , external . Because they are classed as motorised quadri-cycles. Four-wheel mopeds in other words.
Registrations have risen from about 13,000 in 2019 to around 25,000 last year in France.

In Europe, sales have gone from 30,000 to 60,000 in the past five years. And the Ami, launched in 2020, has really changed the image, with teenagers who now account for a quarter of all mini-car sales.
In Selena's very small Citroën, we are soon rolling along at the top speed of 45km/h (28mph). For other road users, no-licence cars like this can seem like mobile traffic calming.
"When I'm on faster roads and there's a lot of traffic the cars behind me sometimes honk their horns but I can't go any quicker!" Selena says.
Daniel Laprès says the Aixam car was "the exact solution to our problem"
Another local Daniel Laprès, who drives a micro-car made by French firm and market-leader Aixam, tells me he actually pulls over to let the cars behind pass.

He and his wife moved from Paris to this country village two years ago. Of Canadian nationality, he didn't swap his foreign licence for a French one in time and lost the right to drive. That didn't matter much when he was in Paris. Like many Parisians he didn't need a car. He used public transport. But that's not possible here.

"We tried living off of taxis and it was in the end a disaster. Then we heard about how you could drive without having to have a licence, and it was the exact solution to our problem. Cheap, inexpensive to operate, basically no administrative formalities, you get insurance."
However, Laprès feels less safe in his small car. "They're little more than tin cans on wheels, right? I mean, you're not going to be driving fast, but someone else could be."
These cars are forbidden on motorways and on faster highways.
By mistake Laprès found himself on a main road with a 110km/h speed limit, which slow vehicles are not allowed on.
"I did it once and I will never, ever do it again. On those roads everybody is passing you, including the biggest trucks. And they come at you very fast from the rear, so it's scary," Laprès says.
Daniel is 77 so fits in with the long-established market for these cars: older people living in the countryside.

Traditionally the market also included quite a few people who'd lost their licences, often because of drink-driving offences. But the launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 changed the customer profile and the product.

"The launch of the Ami was the beginning of the transformation of the sector, with more and more electric models coming on to the market. In 2026, more than 67% of new licence-free cars are electric," says Marie-Laure Nivot, market analyst at AAA Data.
The launch of the Citroën Ami in 2020 "transformed the sector" analysts say
This tendency was encouraged by stricter EU regulations on motorised two-wheelers that had been the vehicles of choice for European teenagers until then.

"It proved too costly for manufacturers to apply the new EU rules, so mopeds and small scooters have almost disappeared from the market since 2020 and licence-free cars have taken their place," Marie-Laure Nivot says.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c689: As the market bell rang out at the Nasdaq today, the Nvidia super-bounce faded.
Its shares slid and are down almost 30% over the past six months, well before the scandal involving Jensen Huang emerged earlier this month.
The legitimate fears about the staying power of the tech boom pre-dated Huang's exit. They have not gone away with his return.

Investors are jittery. Already Anthropic is now trading notably lower than last week's stock market flotation. The firm is the first purely AI company to be publicly listed, and is being seen as a big test for continued investor appetite for the technology.

President Trump's extraordinary phone call to CNBC taking credit for telling the board to reinstate Huang showed the extent of the operation - of some in Silicon Valley and within the US administration - to get him back at the helm.
Among the truly astonishing reflections from President Trump was a suggestion that a two-day investigation of allegations was done and had cleared Huang of national security concerns.
The President said his remarkable move to intervene was because Huang is a "national treasure" who has the next generation of AI chips "in his head". Trump says this is why he needed to act.

In markets, those sceptical about the AI boom say they have never seen an operation to prop up a stock market boom like this. The bond vigilantes and short sellers are now up against Silicon Valley and the White House.
Investors are trading not revenue numbers but levels of political support at a time when US voters have just delivered a backlash against AI data centres.
Against this backdrop, the recovery of the central cash-generating foundation of the tech boom - Nvidia and its $400bn (£304bn) annual sales of advanced chips - looks politically fragile.
This worsens other uncertainties and risks, such as Nvidia's central role in the web of financing, borrowing and cross-ownership to support every corner of the build out of data centres.
The brief interim Nvidia chief executive Colette Kress had already signalled a rowing back from elements of this strategy last week. Where is that now?
The fall back in Anthropic's share price also raises questions about OpenAI's planned listing on the stock exchange. Ultimately these two companies might be the most critical part of all this.

They remain valuable companies with phenomenal technology relied on by the world's biggest companies. The real question is whether that reliance eases, as corporations eschew expensive frontier models for cheaper generic models offered by China.
In turn, all this could be affected by the political backlash, to which the Nvidia psychodrama now contributes.
It is simply not normal to have trillion dollar swings in the value of individual companies.
The extraordinary volatility shows the fragile mood of investors.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9gk: I've just spent a week using Muse, Meta's AI agent that rolls out in the UK today.
Agents are systems that don't just respond to questions but can carry out tasks for you. With Muse, Meta gives the examples of "searching for a cheaper energy deal" or "sorting the school calendar."
And it's true that it has helped me run my life - but it also challenged my personal privacy boundaries, and made me endure some cringeworthy interactions.
It has made a truly enormous bet on AI - of the $145bn (£111bn) it will spend this year much of it will be on building out the tech.

For that to pay off we all need to start using it much more, and Meta hopes Muse will do for AI agents what WhatsApp did for messaging - that is, become the AI agent of choice for billions of people, putting Meta at the forefront of the AI revolution.
But it's not just about what consumers think. Regulators are keeping a careful eye on these emerging tools too.
"Agentic AI has significant potential to benefit people and businesses", the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) noted as Muse launched in the UK.

But its chief executive, Paul Arnold, added it had been "clear with Meta about its responsibilities under data protection law prior to launch, particularly the requirement to ensure that users and the wider public can meaningfully understand and control how their personal data is used in the Muse product".
Muse bills itself as a personal AI agent available to anyone aged 18 and over.
"It doesn't just answer questions, it actually goes out and does work for you," said David Singleton, Meta's VP of engineering on AI products.
"So it helps people stay on top of things," he added. "[It] helps you take tasks and projects off your plate, and also helps you turn your long-term goals into action plans."

What this means is you can set it up to do something for you, like find some specific holiday options, and it will work away on that even as you move off the app and get on with your day, reporting back once it has finished.
It won't book the holiday without your permission - but it can then make the purchase, if you let it.
And the permission requests keep on coming. Every time Muse wants to do something, send something or post something, you have to allow it.

It is reassuring to know that an AI agent isn't running amok in your name, even if it also gets a bit annoying, though you can give it more autonomy (and so get fewer messages) if you adjust the settings.
Muse can't access many apps at the moment but the fundamental ones are the most personal.
I found myself wincing as I hooked it up to one of my personal email accounts, my personal calendar and my personal phone messages. I did not allow it any access to my BBC accounts.
It can't access WhatsApp except to set up a separate chat between it and the user, and while it found me some train tickets, it could not book them via the app which I use, and which is cheaper.

Amazon has blocked it from its marketplace, citing data security concerns but my agent didn't seem to know that, and spent a fruitless hour repeatedly telling me it was still waiting for the page to load in order to find me some shelves.
A number of big UK firms are working with Meta though, including Marks & Spencer, Debenhams Group, Currys, Sainsbury's and Ocado.
The ICO is urging consumers to be cautious with AI agents though: "consider the pros and cons," it said in a blog post to coincide with Muse's launch. , external
"Agents can make mistakes. Mistakes can be magnified if the agent is acting autonomously," it noted.
Meta is keen to emphasise how its agents can be personalised: "No two Muses are alike," , external it says in its press release.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/tennis/artic: Alcaraz sends Spain to the final with dominant win against Fery
Great Britain were unable to give Leon Smith the perfect send-off as Davis Cup captain as Carlos Alcaraz inspired Spain to a 2-0 victory in the semi-finals.

Competing in their first Davis Cup semi-final since 2019, Britain fell short as Arthur Fery was unable to match the dazzling brilliance of Alcaraz, with the seven-time major winner surging to an emphatic 6-2 6-1 win.
That was after rising star Rafael Jodar defeated Cameron Norrie 6-2 7-5 in the opening singles match to put Spain in the driving seat in Bologna.
The defeat brings the curtain down on Smith's near 17-year tenure as captain, during which he led Britain to Davis Cup success in 2015.

Spain captain David Ferrer, who is also stepping down after this year's tournament, will have the chance to guide his nation to their first Davis Cup title since 2019 when they face Italy in Sunday's final.
Italy are the three-time defending champions, although they are without talisman and world number two Jannik Sinner because of injury.
After Norrie's defeat by Jodar, Fery was faced with the mammoth task of beating world number three Alcaraz - a player he had never faced before.
Alcaraz lifted his first ATP Finals title six days earlier, a triumph that completed his astonishing return to the sport following four months out with a wrist injury.
And his return to top form was on full display as he dismantled Fery, ranked 32nd, in a dominant first set in which he dropped just two points behind his first serve.
Alcaraz's movement and shot-making continued to dazzle the crowd in Italy and Fery could do little to stop the Spaniard's sprint to the finish line.

Alcaraz started the season by becoming the youngest man to complete the career Grand Slam with his Australian Open triumph, and now has the chance to end the year with his first Davis Cup title, one of the few trophies he has yet to win.

For Fery, who enjoyed his career-best season and a fairytale run to the Wimbledon semi-finals, it was another harsh reminder of the gulf in class between himself and the game's top players after he fell in straight sets to world number one Alexander Zverev in Thursday's quarter-final.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Cole Palmer left the City Ground without having a shot or a touch in the opposition box as Chelsea lost 3-2 at Nottingham Forest on Friday night.

The 24-year-old forward started the season by registering six goal involvements in his first six league games (two goals and four assists), but his penalty against Manchester United is now his only goal contribution in the past six matches.
Last weekend, after his side were booed off following the 4-1 defeat by Leeds United , Palmer appeared reluctant to take part in the customary post-match acknowledgement of the supporters.

Chelsea have lost their past three games. They have conceded 23 goals in their opening 12 Premier League matches, their highest total at this stage since the 2015-16 season, with Alonso facing criticism for the leaky defence and constant line-up changes .
One positive had been the attack, with Chelsea scoring 18 times in six matches, largely because of the link-up play between Palmer, Morgan Rogers and Joao Pedro.
However, that has dropped off. Club-record signing Rogers, who cost £117m in the summer, has also become less effective, while Joao Pedro is sidelined for now by a groin injury.
Some observers argue Palmer needs to step up to help lift his team out of this difficult period.
It is nearly two years since he produced the form of his life, breaking Chelsea 's Premier League record with 39 goal involvements (26 goals and 13 assists) in the 2024 calendar year.
There are no concerns about Palmer's attitude or behaviour internally at Chelsea .
Senior sources inside the club say he has been ultra-focused behind the scenes, doing extra sessions and he is described as a "leader" by Alonso.

In mid-April, deep into a dismal campaign in which Chelsea finished 10th having had three different managers, rumours were rife he was pining for a return to Manchester, with United - a club he still supports - linked.

When speaking to the Guardian, he added: "All my family are there, but I don't miss it. Maybe I'll miss it if I don't go for three months or something. But then when I get home I think there's nothing there for me anyway. I've got no plans to move from Chelsea ."
A move to United was never seriously explored by any of those involved and Palmer re-established his commitment to Chelsea by signing a lucrative deal until 2034.
It made him among the club's highest-paid players and followed similar deals for Reece James, Moises Caicedo and Joao Pedro.
Palmer's mother, father and girlfriend were all present in the directors' box against Bournemouth after he signed the new deal.

Like the others who have recently renewed, Palmer has been reassured by the sporting leadership team that Chelsea are ambitious, out to win trophies and have learned from past mistakes, hiring a high-calibre manager in Alonso and signing three over-30 players for the first time in four years to add experience to their squad.
That said, Palmer has not hit the heights of his first 18 months under former manager Mauricio Pochettino, now in charge of Manchester United , and then early into Enzo Maresca's reign.
Having been nicknamed "Cold" Palmer after his goal celebration, where he shrugs his shoulders and pretends to be cold, his decline began in early 2025.
Liverpool kept back-to-back clean sheets under Andoni Iraola for the first time this week
A year has passed, and there has been a world of change at Liverpool .
Thursday marked 12 months since the Reds lost 4-1 to PSV Eindhoven at Anfield in the Champions League, the culmination of their worst run of results in more than 70 years.
By the time the final whistle blew that night there were some boos, but Anfield was half empty and belief from the fanbase had evaporated as Liverpool lost for the ninth time in 12 games.

Arne Slot's side had won the Premier League title the season before, but that game against the Dutch side was arguably the nadir of his second campaign in charge. Steven Gerrard said that evening that Liverpool "just keep bleeding".
The bleeding did stop somewhat, and Liverpool qualified for the Champions League, but it was a campaign that left Slot wounded and, come the end of the campaign, he was sacked.
Everyone has moved on in one way or another. The PSV game is in the distant past now.

And after a dizzying few days where Liverpool have scored seven without reply across the Premier League and Champions League, beating Manchester United and Club Brugge, Andoni Iraola's side are giving fans reasons to start believing again.
That is just as well, because Sunday is derby day against Everton .
"You can really see this manager stamping his philosophy and his way of playing on the team," former Liverpool captain Gerrard said on BBC Radio 5 Live this week.
"They are playing a lot faster, a lot more intense, playing a lot more vertical and getting it forward a lot quicker.
"It's a lot more exciting to watch than it was at the back end of last season."

When Liverpool lost to Arsenal at the start of November, they were threatening in phases against the reigning champions but finished the game without a shot on target - despite starting with three attacking players who cost more than £100m each.
But they have now scored 10 goals in their past three games, with that trio of Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola delivering 10 goal involvements between them.

Both Isak and Wirtz are in their best form since making the move to Liverpool in 2025 and both spoke in Bruges this week about how good they are feeling. Isak has four goals in his past four matches while Wirtz has scored in each of his past three.
"Under Iraola, he has given him more freedom, more licence to take risks and to be the difference maker."

Combined, Wirtz and Isak have surpassed their total goal involvements from last season and, alongside the likes of Barcola, Cody Gakpo, Victor Munoz, Rio Ngumoha and Hugo Ekitike - once he returns from injury in January - Liverpool have a youthful and vibrant attack that can rattle fear into defences across Europe.
"It's not just about those two [Isak and Wirtz]. If we play well, someone will score," said Iraola. "If we have more chances then the opposition, someone will score."
Iraola will also be pleased that his midfielders are getting high up the pitch and scoring too, with Alexis Mac Allister and Dominik Szoboszlai getting nine goals between them this season.

The challenge now is for the frontline to deliver consistently and crucially, in those games against the best opposition. In the Champions League, Liverpool have scored 17 times in five games, but it hasn't gone unnoticed that they failed to score once across 180 minutes against Manchester City and Arsenal .

Like he did against LASK, Iraola opted to rest Virgil van Dijk against Club Brugge and the centre-back duo of Jeremy Jacquet and Ronald Araujo helped to keep a clean sheet. From the eye test alone, Liverpool are looking more assured defensively and Araujo's ability to fill in across the backline is a big part of that.
How a football team rebuilt after 19 players died in plane crash
It was 2am when Ivan Tozzo picked up his mobile phone and heard his football club's secretary screaming his name.
A plane carrying the Chapecoense team had crashed into a mountain.
Seventy-one people were dead, including 19 of 22 players from the Brazilian club who were on their way to the biggest game in their history.
It would later emerge the plane had run out of fuel and investigators would find the airline and pilot were to blame as the fuel load was insufficient for the flight on 28 November 2016.
But in the early hours, as Tozzo watched the TV news in the changing room at the club's stadium, his only thought was for the players who would not be coming back to this room.
When he sat alone in the club's boardroom after the funerals as the only director still alive, he cried.
That was the moment when Tozzo – who had changed his mind about travelling with the team because he had a sense of unease about the trip - decided he would lead Chapecoense to rise again.
Ivan Tozzo recalls the phone call he got after the crash: "It was our club secretary, Jorilda, who was desperate, screaming 'Ivan Ivan'."
Chapecoense had been travelling to Colombia to play Atletico Nacional of Medellin in the first leg of the Copa Sudamericana final, South America's second most prestigious club tournament.
"The team was very motivated, knowing that we were engraving our names inside the history of the club," goalkeeper Jakson Follmann, one of the three surviving players, tells BBC Sport.
Aged 24 at the time, Follmann had also been looking forward to his imminent wedding, little knowing he would be spending two months in hospital instead.
"Everyone was completely proud of everything they were doing, both for the team and for the community of Chapeco and the region," Follmann says.

Commentator Rafael Henzel, who was one of six survivors of the crash but who died in 2019 following a heart attack, described the Copa Sudamericana as the team's "World Cup" and said in 2017 that "if anyone's ever died happy, it was the people on that plane".
Survivors Neto, Alan Ruschel, Follmann and Henzel (left to right) appeared together at a friendly between Brazil and Colombia two months after the crash

The LaMia 2933 flight from Santa Cruz in Bolivia to the Colombian city of Medellin had a journey distance similar to the plane's flying range, but it did not stop to refuel and crashed into a mountain just 18km from its intended destination.

The pilot, Miguel Quiroga, who was also a co-owner of the airline, died in the crash. In a leaked tape, he can be heard warning of a "total electric failure" and "lack of fuel". However, he did not make a formal distress call.

A Bolivian investigation concluded that the pilot and the airline were directly responsible for the crash, while a Colombian investigation said there was no technical failure and blamed the pilot, the airline and Bolivian regulators.
"I don't call it an accident, I say it was a crime that could have been avoided," says Follman, whose right leg had to be partially amputated to save his life.
"It's the crime of not stopping to refuel, the greed to think that he [the pilot] could get there... with the fuel practically finished."
To date, no-one has been found guilty in relation to the crash.
At the time, Bolivia did not have a system for prosecuting companies. Even when such a facility was introduced in 2021, it did not cover negligent homicide or causing an air disaster.

Charges were brought against individuals in LaMia's management - who denied wrongdoing - but in 2020 a trial was delayed by jurisdictional disputes and difficulties involving defendants who were abroad.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/articles/c61: Zak (left), Luca (centre) and Freddy (right) Carrick-Smith on the podium in New Zealand
Three Britons on a skiing podium, the union jack emblazoned across their race bibs as they lift their skis in celebration.

At a slalom race in New Zealand in September, Luca, Freddy and Zak Carrick-Smith completed a sibling clean sweep of the medals, something no three brothers are believed to have ever done before in the history of FIS alpine skiing.
"It was super special," Freddy tells BBC Sport. "The goal is to do the same thing at a World Cup or the Olympics now."
Their success came at the start of a winter season in which the brothers hope to solidify their burgeoning potential as British alpine skiing's next big things.
And could they follow in the grooves of Olympians Graham and Martin Bell, and Alain and Noel Baxter, to become GB's next family skiing dynasty?
Freddy, 19, is on GB's World Cup squad, while his twin Zak and older brother Luca, 21, are on the second-tier Europa Cup team.
And with their parents as their coaches, it is a full family affair.
The boys' mother Emma Carrick-Anderson was a four-time Winter Olympian for Team GB, while father Phil Smith founded Snoworks ski courses, which operate across Europe.
"They know us best, so they know us much better than just a random coach would," says Zak.
"And then as brothers, me and Freddy have been racing our whole lives together, pushing each other, and then Luca ahead pushing us too. I think that's why we've got so far."
Luca adds: "The best part of it probably, for us, is the competition, and I always want to be the best in everything, especially when we grew up.
"Everything you did, you'd always be pushing harder and harder. We all get along really well, and it's just like being with your best friends all the time.
"It's always been pretty incredible, but it has been difficult at times."
While Luca (back right) was born in Scotland, twins Freddy (front left) and Zak (front centre) were born in France and the trio were raised in the Alps
Emma is matter-of-fact about that challenge. Asked what was behind the decision to go it alone as a family, she said: "Basically we didn't have a choice. Ski racing is incredibly expensive.
"When the boys were young, it was all just fun. I don't think we really planned that we were going to take this journey to where we are now, knocking on the World Cup door.

"We would never have been able to afford to put them in an academy. So I think we were lucky, I was an ex-ski racer, Phil was a ski racer, we were also ski coaches, so we could do it ourselves. Not all families are quite as lucky."
Each season, they must source about £320,000. Last season, they feared they would run out of money by mid-January.
While some of their funding comes through GB Snowsport and its Alpine Foundation, the rest must be found through sponsorship deals and crowdfunding campaigns.
When BBC Sport speaks to Emma, she is in Colorado with Freddy, where he will race in the giant slalom World Cup this weekend.

There, a two-and-a-half-hour training session on the slopes costs $1,200 (£914). Fortunately, they are able to split that cost with other teams, but with Luca in Finland and Zak in Austria, Emma and Phil - who quit their jobs a number of years ago - effectively run three different programmes.
Emma Carrick-Anderson competed at the 1992, 1994, 1998 and 2002 Winter Olympics for Great Britain
Coaches, ski techs, fitness instructors, course-setters, drivers, cooks - they have done plenty of jobs on their sons' journeys up the rankings.

Emma describes them as completely different personalities, and yet "all incredibly determined in their own way". But managing the emotions of her three sons as they learn to navigate the ups and downs of professional sport has been the parents' hardest role.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Steward has scored 11 tries in 45 Test appearances for England
England's Freddie Steward says he is determined to play his own game as he starts against New Zealand on Saturday ahead of full-back rival George Furbank.
Furbank put in impressive play-making performances in wins over the All Blacks and Australia this autumn, stepping into first receiver and linking play out wide.
Steward has different strengths. The Leicester man is a huge aerial presence under the high ball and a powerful rangy runner.

While the 25-year-old has also developed other areas of his game, noticeably laying on a try for Will Joseph with a superbly weighted grubber kick against Japan, Steward has learned to be confident in his own abilities, rather than be concerned about comparisons.
"I've probably been guilty in the last couple of opportunities of trying to prove something or be someone that I'm not," Steward told 5 Live Breakfast.
"Against Japan I said to myself I just want to go play with a smile on my face and actually just go and enjoy it and be who I am.
Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Sounds, BBC Sport website and app

With Marcus Smith's ability to play full-back, along with his more accustomed fly-half, making him a more versatile bench option, Steward's only route into the England matchday squad would appear to be as the starting full-back.

It is a role he made his own after making his debut against the United States in July 2021. He started every game in the following two Six Nations campaigns and was first choice through England's run to the semi-finals at the 2023 Rugby World Cup.

However, he was dropped from the starting line-up in favour of Furbank in the middle of the 2024 Six Nations. His emotional phonecall telling his girlfriend that he was out of the team was captured in the Full Contact Netflix documentary that covered the tournament.

With Smith and Elliot Daly also given opportunities at full-back, Steward has had to battle for his position and overcome set-backs. He was substituted in the first half of England's 42-21 defeat by Ireland in February.
But he says working with a psychologist and avoiding social media reviews of his performances have helped power an excellent start to the current campaign with table-topping Tigers.
"When I first started working with psychologists, I was probably quite young and I really didn't appreciate the mental side of the game," Steward added.

"But I think the more you experience things like being dropped, you actually need to work on the mental side of it; how you react to those situations, how you deal with pressure, how you come back from those hurdles.
"It's been a long and winding road, but I just feel like I've learned so much. It's been a massive education for me.
"I go nowhere near that [social media comments] now. That was a lesson I learned pretty early on.
"You jump online, you're going to see some stuff that isn't nice reading. That's just the way it is in the world we live in now.
"What matters is the fans who turn up every week to watch us, the coach, my family, my team-mates. They're the people I do it for."

Steward says his mother finds it too hard to watch him leap for high balls. It is an area which is more fiercely contested than ever, with a law tweak having made it easier for chasing players to get into the same airspace and battle for possession.
Steward is treated on the pitch during his debut against the United States in 2021

"It is scary. I won't be afraid to admit it," said Steward. "No, it's terrifying. The ball goes up and it is pretty much now a complete free-for-all. You've just got to launch yourself up in the air, try and bring it down and, unfortunately, you don't have time to look at everyone else.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/art: Dip, swerve, curl, whip. Hours spent mastering the craft of a great free-kick ensure those that ripple the back of the net are particularly satisfying.
This week we are digging into the Premier League's all-time best takers.

The number of goals scored from direct free-kicks has gradually decreased over the past two decades (boo!) with a rising focus on generating higher-quality chances, rather than having a pop from range.

It is perhaps unsurprising then that James Maddison is the only current player in the competition's all-time top 25 free-kick scorers, after James Ward-Prowse returned to Championship side Southampton in the summer.
Dominik Szoboszlai, however, is bucking the trend with five since joining Liverpool from 32 attempts - an impressive conversion rate of 15.6% and almost a third of his total Premier League goals.
He looks on course to become a free-kick great, already only one goal behind Trent Alexander-Arnold and Leighton Baines and just two off the likes of Matt le Tissier, Wayne Rooney and Steven Gerrard.
The majority of top scorers hail from the halcyon era of, essentially, having a dig.
Yaya Toure belongs in another category - he misses out on the top 10 below but could be deemed a 'one-season wonder' in this realm, despite having eight years at Manchester City .

His prolific spell in 2013-14 deserves recognition, scoring four of his seven free-kick attempts that term - a staggering 57.1% conversion rate and by far the Premier League's best since Opta began collecting such data in 2006.

There is also an honourable mention for Louis Saha, the only man in the Premier League era to score a free-kick with each foot - with his left for Manchester United against Southampton in January 2004, and with his right for Everton against Fulham seven years later.
And while we are here, these are the goalkeepers who least liked facing them.
What we are looking for, though, are the real free-kick specialists - those players whose names evoke memories of ball meeting top bins.

For that reason, despite sitting joint-third on the scorers list with 12, Cristiano Ronaldo and Thierry Henry do not make it. They just scored too many goals - and too many great ones - to be renowned specifically for their set-pieces.
Fewer than 7% of Henry's 175 Premier League goals were free-kicks, netting one on average every 21.5 games. Ronaldo, meanwhile, tried his luck 167 times, scoring one roughly every 14 attempts.

The first spot up for grabs could have gone several ways - Maddison, as mentioned, has a decent shout to be included, and likewise Christian Eriksen who netted eight in the Premier League and also laid on 13 free-kick assists.
Frank Lampard has nine goals but also the most attempts on record - and the data only accounts for half his Premier League career.
Ashley Young is the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick
OK, the case for Ashley Young is in his longevity - he curled in a free-kick during the play-offs to help Watford win promotion in 2006 and was still scoring them almost two decades later.

At 39 years and 148 days old, Young became the oldest player to score a Premier League free-kick in Everton 's win over Wolves in December 2024. His seventh successful free-kick strike in the competition and the final effort of his 50-goal top-flight haul.
Young holds a decent conversion rate, scoring with 10.3% of his 68 top-flight attempts, while also chipping in with nine free-kick assists - only a handful of players have more since 2003-04.

Young's set-piece duties also tend to bookend his career. A trusted specialist at Watford and Aston Villa , he fell behind Ronaldo, Rooney and co at United but still popped up with a memorable long-range free-kick against the Hornets, his boyhood club.

Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana was subjected to repeated boos and told "you're not welcome here" by his own fans during Friday's Premier League defeat by Nottingham Forest .
The jeers aimed at the 25-year-old were heard every time he touched the ball and came after an unauthorised interview with French YouTuber Zach Nani was released.
In that controversial two-hour conversation, Fofana also appeared to joke about missing his penalty during last month's Carabao Cup shootout defeat by Liverpool .
Manager Xabi Alonso said the French centre-back had apologised and "it won't be repeated".
But Fofana endured a difficult time in his side's trip to Forest as supporters made their feelings known.
After Chelsea went behind to a brilliant volley from Igor Jesus in the fifth minute, Fofana also conceded a penalty for the home side's second goal from Morgan Gibbs-White in the 51st minute.

He was booked for the foul on Liam Delap in the box, and then replaced by Levi Colwill in the 56th minute - just after Emmanuel Emegha had pulled a goal back for the visitors - before Gibbs-White made it 3-1 in the 72nd minute.
Emegha scored again in the 89th minute to make it 3-2, but Forest held on to secure their first win over Chelsea at the City Ground since 1997.
Alonso defended Fofana after the game and said in his post-match news conference: "We have to stick together, and everyone that is in the changing room, everyone in the team is needed.
"We need to help, and we need to go through these tough moments all together, and we don't leave anyone apart.
"We need to support everyone. That is because we need everyone, and we need the fans.
"We need all the players. We need to stick together because if not, things will get more complicated, and that's what we want to do."
Asked whether the reaction of the Chelsea fans will make it difficult to pick Fofana going forward, he added: "Well, I'm thinking right after the game, and for the next games, we will see."
Wesley Fofana has made 10 appearances for Chelsea this season
Meanwhile, Nani has moved to defend Fofana, saying the player was "clearly" not happy during the interview and admitted he had to perform better.
Fofana also explained he opted to take a penalty against Liverpool as one of the senior players on the pitch, having joined in a £75m move from Leicester City in 2022.
But he confessed football had reached a stage where he was "more unhappy than happy", before recovering physically and mentally.
The release of the interview has coincided with the club's poor run of form, with Chelsea losing 4-1 at home to Leeds United last weekend to make it three defeats in four matches.
The defence, in particular, has come in for criticism, with the Blues one of four clubs to have conceded more than 20 goals in the Premier League after 11 matches.
Having been subjected to racist abuse in the past, Fofana spoke about handling comments during a club-organised interview on this summer's pre-season tour of Asia.
He is understood to be one of the highest earners at Stamford Bridge.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/: Codie Taylor led the New Zealand haka against England before the 37-12 defeat last Saturday
Despite a population, player pool and bank balance smaller than most of their rivals, New Zealand's rugby team have become sporting shorthand for success.
England beat the All Blacks this year and last. They play them again on Saturday aiming for a hat-trick.
But, England would need that winning streak to continue until around 2050 just to level up a lop-sided historical head-to-head.
New Zealand have won 36 times to England's 10 in their 121-year rivalry.
For every other nation in Test rugby, the story is the same. New Zealand have the superior record against them all.
A section on the All Blacks' website, titled Rivalries, , external opens by listing South Africa's 40% winning record in their meetings. And the numbers only drop from there.
But New Zealand's grip on the global game appears looser now than ever.
If they lose to England on Saturday, it may not much sway the historical balance between the two teams.

But it would be a sixth defeat in a calendar year, a total matched only once before in the All Blacks past, back in 1949 when a split squad played two Test series in Australia and apartheid South Africa at the same time.
New Zealand's win percentage in 2026 is 58.3%, their third lowest for any year since the start of professionalism.
This campaign, marked by an exhausting schedule and four Tests away to the world champion Springboks, is in keeping with a recent trend.
Since the end of the 2010s - a period in which an all-time great team captured back-to-back world titles - New Zealand have come off the boil.
The 2020s are on course to be their least successful decade since the 1970s.
This current crop of All Blacks are suffering not just by comparison to the previous generation, but when set against every other modern predecessor.
The All Blacks' culture of promoting within and establishing coaching dynasties was seen as key when they were winning.

A thread ran through the Graham Henry, Steve Hansen and Ian Foster succession in the 2010s glory days. The latter two served under their predecessor and the first two earned their Test stripes with Wales, before taking the top job.
All were schooled as coaches in New Zealand and steeped in the country's rugby traditions.
The in-house production line of leaders ensured continuity and protected a team ethos that has been admired and written about everywhere.
But, in a modern world in which opposition tactics are quickly picked apart and best practice spreads fast, has adherence to tradition held back the team?
New Zealand's rivals have all hired coaching talent from outside.

Rassie Erasmus, South African to the core, may front the Springbok coaching operation, but behind him Irishmen Jerry Flannery and Felix Jones and Tony Brown, a former All Black himself, bring specialist knowledge to different areas.
France, famously patriotic in their hiring, benefited from Englishman Shaun Edwards and South African Vlok Cilliers' work behind the scenes in recent years.
England, Ireland, Scotland and Wales all have or have had head coaches from other countries.

Dave Rennie, who has coached Australia, Glasgow Warriors and Japanese side Kobe Steelers previously, became the first person of Pasifika heritage to lead the All Blacks when he took on the job in March.
He has brought a Scottish contingent to mix up his backroom, with attack coach Mike Blair the most high-profile.
But his regime is still only eight months old. Other issues predate it.

The Black Caps hold the strong upper hand over India after the second day of the second cricket test at Hagley Oval, Christchurch.
Starting the day at 246/5, the Black Caps added another 110 runs, before being dismissed in the second session, and then had India reeling at 116/6 at stumps, still 240 runs in arrears.
New Zealand scored 356, with wicketkeeper Tom Blundell leading the way with 89, before he was the ninth batter out, as he hit out at the Indian bowling attack.
He struck 10 boundaries in his 211-ball innings and had solid support down the order from Glenn Phillips, who was out early on Saturday for 36, Nathan Smith, Kyle Jamieson and Matt Henry.
Akash Deep took his fifth wicket for the day, when Henry was last man out for 19.
Henry was straight back into the action, snaring Indian opener Yashasvi Jaiswal for a duck with the last ball of the first over of India's innings.
Jamieson followed up soon after, having Devdutt Padikkal caught behind by Blundell for 21, and India, who racked up 720/9 in their first innings of the drawn test in Wellington, looked much shakier.
Jamieson boosted the Black Caps further, tempting India captain Shubman Gill into an edge that Tom Latham gratefully snaffled at second slip.
That left India 59/3 at tea, but with dangerman Rishabh Pant at the crease. The Wellington centurion had scored 23, when he tried to slog Jacob Duffy out of the park, but was caught by Jamieson.
Duffy claimed the fifth wicket, when opener KL Rahul speared a ball to Devon Conway at point.
Then just before stumps, Washington Sundar edged one to Latham, leaving his team in big trouble, as the Kiwi pace bowlers starred with a sterling performance.
Duffy took 2/21, a welcome rebound, after he became the first New Zealand bowler to concede 200-plus runs in a single test innings at the Basin Reserve last week.
He said he really enjoyed the crowd supporting the bowlers on Saturday.
"The first half was really good to get to a competitive total, on the back of Tommy's [Blundell's] bat," he told Sky Sport.
Then, when the New Zealanders were bowling, the Canterbury crowd got behind them.
"They had a few beers by the end of it and they were getting pretty rowdy. It was good fun."
Duffy, who was named today in the New Zealand squad for the four-test series against Australia, said he had battling a few demons with his bowling action lately.
"So to get a bit of luck go your way, it's actually quite nice."

When Australian rugby league star Reece Walsh asked, "How's that for culture, baby?" after the Kangaroos' Rugby League World Cup final win , his comments sparked a wider conversation about culture in the game.
Australia had just beaten the Kiwis 32-12 in Brisbane, with a passionate Walsh responding to criticism of his team and its supporters throughout the tournament.
"Coming into this tournament everybody wrote us off, talking about how good the other teams are, how good their cultures are, I just feel we got disrespected," he told Australias Channel 7.
"Seeing all the fans come out, how's that for culture, baby?"
Kiwis captain James Fisher Harris shares a hongi with fellow Warriors teammate and Tonga winger Dallin Watene‑Zelezniak.

His comments landed at a tournament where cultural identity is impossible to ignore. From the haka, siva tau and sipi tau to the parades held across nations, supporters and players proudly represented their whakapapa and country.

Māori artist Charles Williams (Ngāti Kahungunu ki te Wairoa, Te Whakatohea, Tūhoe, Ngāpuhi), who was at the centre of many Kiwi parades and celebrations in Aotearoa told RNZ that without culture the Rugby League World Cup would be "boring as heck."
"This campaign for the RLWC has really been a highlight on cultures , on the uniqueness of different nations. I think more than ever before, it's come to the forefront."
Williams said the competition and sporting bodies "really need to tap into it".
"This is what makes the competition. Basically, without culture, Rugby League World Cup will be boring as heck.
"I don't think they'll get as many views, bums on seats, money invested in the entire tournament. And so it's just like, come on, man, you're right there."
Toa Samoa after overcoming Tonga for a 34-6 victory at Brisbane's Suncorp Stadium in October 2025.
Williams said that after a long rugby league season, people "want to belong".
"There needs to be something that picks you up and it has to be deeper than money. You know, it has to be a purpose."
A match between Fiji and the Cook Islands at McDonald Jones Stadium in Newcastle, Sunday, 18 October 12026.

For Worimi man Isaac Frederick Maynard, the conversation that followed Walsh's comments around culture raised questions about how Australian sport recognised its own First Nations cultures, and whether that recognition went far enough.

Maynard, who was born and raised on Wiradjuri Country in central New South Wales, told RNZ that history and connection to Country were important when considering what people meant when they talk about Australian culture.
'Country' was similar to a persons tūrangawaewae or "a place to stand" in te ao Māori, it referred to the land or ancestral place where a person was descended from.
"When we're talking about what people are calling Australian culture, it's important to remember that we're 125 years since Federation, right? So it's a short time period."
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have the world's oldest continuing cultures.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples had the world's oldest continuing cultures, with cultural connections stretching back more than 65,000 years.
There were hundreds of distinct First Nations communities across Australia, each with their own languages, customs, laws and cultural practices.
Maynard said the cultural pride displayed by Māori and Pacific teams at the World Cup stood out to him.

"We thought he had a strong game against Wales and off the bench last week, and so we are keen for him to have a crack."
Despite his move to the bench, Rennie said Roigard can still have a significant impact on the game.
"Bringing Cam's experience on late in the game, we think it will work for us."
While the All Blacks were off the pace in almost every aspect of their record 37-12 loss to England last week , Rennie pointed to their kicking game as one area that needs improvement.
