Coach Dave Rennie said Jordie Barrett was the natural choice as All Blacks captain for this weekend's rematch with England at Twickenham.

Hooker and tour skipper Codie Taylor is one of four players ruled out of the game with injury, opening the door for Jordie to become the third Barrett brother to lead the All Blacks, after Scott and Beauden.

"I think anyone who would have worked with Jordie would know he's very impressive, great game understanding, both sides of the ball, he's prepared to challenge and he's been great in our leadership group."
"He's taken over the captaincy role when Codie has left the field last week and a couple of weeks ago, so, it was a pretty straightforward decision for us."
Rennie has made six changes to his starting XV, some injury enforced, with Taylor , midfielder Anton Lienert-Brown, forward Tupou Vaa'i and wing Will Jordan all unavailable.
Asafo Aumua starts at hooker, Scott Barrett and Fabian Holland are the locks with Anton Segner, Peter Lakai and Wallace Sititi in the loose forwards.

Cortez Ratima and Richie Mo'unga are at halfback and first-five respectively, while Leicester Fainga'anuku joins Jordie Barrett in the centres with Rieko Ioane and Josh Moorby on the wings. Damian McKenzie shifts from No.10 to fullback.

Halfback Cam Roigard and fullback Beauden Barrett drop to the bench, while hooker George Bell, prop Xavier Numia, lock Josh Lord, loose forward Ethan Blackadder and midfielder Timoci Tavatavanawai join the match-day 23.
Richie Mo'unga will start at first-five with Damian McKenzie moving to fullback and Beauden Barrett dropping to the bench.
Rennie said once it was decided Taylor wouldn't play, the front rower wanted to let Barrett know he would be leading the team for the first time.
"I told him we were going to make Jordie captain and he said 'oh can I tell him?'. Codie was quite emotional when he passed that information on to Jordie."
Rennie said it's an "unbelievable" achievement for the Barrett family, but said he made the call to give Jordie the captaincy as he's "the right man for the job."
Rennie said Barrett's challenge will be getting the best out of everyone around him.

"He carries the team on his back. He's the one who flies out and gives you line speed and he chases things, so with the extra responsibility of captaincy, he's going to have to be really good at getting the best of others," Rennie said.
The All Blacks are determined to win at Twickenham on Sunday in the Nations Championship third place playoff and bounce back from consecutive losses to Wales and England .

The All Blacks have now lost five tests this year for just the third time in their history and they won't want to be just the second New Zealand side in history to suffer six defeats in a season. The last time that happened was in 1945.
Rennie said they were their own worst enemies in the record 37-12 defeat to the English, but he is confident they can fix the issues that plagued them last weekend.
"Our line-out's got to be better, the quality of our kicking game has got to be contestable if we're doing that," Rennie said.
"We just weren't clinical enough and made double the amount of errors that England did with half the amount of ball. And then defensively, especially set-piece, just our connection.
"We've put a lot of time into those key things and if we can get that part of the game right, then we'll be in the hunt."

It provides the soundtrack to a pivotal sequence where the game's protagonists get their first taste of the high life - zooming around on jet skis and shooting champagne bottles from the back of a yacht.
"My guilty admission is that I haven't even played the game yet, but I'm excited to try it. I'm gonna become a late-in-life gamer!"
The placement has given the song a new lease of life. Its daily streams rose from 20,000 to 281,000 overnight. On Friday, it re-entered the UK charts at a new peak of 28.
"It's wild," says Jepsen from her home in Los Angeles. "I love a plot twist, and this was exactly that."
In some ways, it’s a vindication for an under-appreciated classic.
"I've always been asked the question, 'When you were in the studio, did you know you had a hit song?'" says Jepsen. "And I always say, 'No. How can anyone know that?'

"However, I will say, with Run Away With Me, out of all the sessions I've ever done in my life, we all felt that thrill that people think you get. We were on our feet, going, 'Oh, this has something special to it'.
"But it never got eyes like it's getting right now, and that makes me believe in that special feeling that we had, when we made it."
The success comes at an interesting juncture in Jepsen’s career.
Over the last decade, Run Away With Me and E•MO•TION, the album it featured on, have become cult classics, helping to establish Jepsen as a favourite among pop connoisseurs.
This year, she rewarded her dedicated fans with a 32-track double album, Day & Night, that spans everything from mellow folk-pop to Abba pastiches and darker, dancefloor-centric experimentation.
It was released as Jepsen, 41, welcomed her first child, Ilya, after falling in love with one of her co-writers, Cole Marsden Greif-Neill, during recording sessions.
She told us more about the music, and her plans for touring with a newborn.
In 2015, E•MO•TION was considered a commercial disappointment – but now it's considered a landmark pop album. How do you look back at it now?

At the time, I remember feeling the pressure of having a song like Call Me Maybe take off. I was nervous about people expecting the same on repeat, knowing that I wasn't capable of delivering that. So E•MO•TION, to me, was a statement of like, 'Here's the type of pop music I love, and here's what I have to offer beyond [Call Me Maybe].'

I'd set my expectations low. I'd taken a break and done Cinderella on Broadway. And when I finally put the album out, I was pretty sure everyone had forgotten what I did. So the fact anyone liked it was a victory.

But did I imagine that it would catapult this new career path for me? I had no insight of that and, looking back at it now, I feel like it was like accidentally strategic for my [type of] success, which is finding people who want something true and authentic and artful, versus Call Me Maybe 2.0.
And that freedom led you to a place where you can release a double album.

Oh, absolutely! There are songs on this album that would normally be locked away in folders on my hard drive. On many songs, I felt like, 'Is this too weird?' But the mission statement with Day & Night was to stop asking that question.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqly: "The difficult part was deciding whether to release it or not."
Jake Bugg says writing his latest album was an opportunity to explore loss, regrets and the lessons he has learned along the way.
After enjoying success with his self-titled debut album in 2012, the Nottingham singer says he has since struggled to maintain relationships and ended up feeling isolated.
Despite such a personal record potentially leaving him "very vulnerable", he decided "if somebody can take a slight bit of comfort in this record then the music's bigger than myself".
Best known for the single Lightning Bolt, Bugg released six albums between 2012 and 2024.
But his latest, Alamo, reflects a difficult period in his life.
Bugg first came to prominence through the BBC Introducing strand
"I don't want to go into too many specifics, but it's a combination of things I struggled with," he told the BBC.

"I'd lost a lot of people close to me in a very short space of time, then came a really tough time with relationships - and trying to keep something like that together, while everything else was going on was very difficult. In the end, it was impossible.
"And then you also have the frustrations with the work side of things as well, and things from childhood that I'm only starting to face.
"Being on your own and trying to make sense of it all and trying, in some ways, to self-medicate.
"So that's the theme of the record: Life builds up and gets the best of us all, sometimes."
Bugg, who grew up on a council estate in the Clifton area of Nottingham, has maintained his links with the city .
But the turmoil of the years since has informed much of this latest record.
He said: "I said a lot of things when I was younger that were just ridiculous, to be honest. When I started, I didn't really know what I was doing really.
"I'd be quite honest about most things, but not necessarily in a positive or a good way. And yeah, I wish I could kind of go back and word things a little bit better."

Bugg continued: "Everywhere I Go is the last song on the record, and it's a bit of a tough listen for me if I'm honest, because it gives me flashbacks to some of these points in my life that that I'm singing about.
"That song is about carrying all of that around with you and not really realising it and the fact you can't ever escape it.
"I've been a bit worried to lean into the darker side, a little bit worried about what people may think. But this record for me allowed me to really go down those rabbit holes."
While struggling with elements of his life, this surprisingly resulted in a more straightforward creative process.
"If anything, it was quite easy and natural because it was so honest," he said.
"The difficult part was deciding whether to release it or not - because it's quite personal and you're leaving yourself very vulnerable.
"But I came to the decision to release the record because I know how much of an impact other people's records had on me growing up.
"I thought, if somebody can take a slight bit of comfort in this record then the music's bigger than myself."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp8: Over a career spanning more than two decades, Gallagher became a familiar face on television, radio and stage
Taoiseach (Irish prime minster) Micheál Martin has led tributes to comedian and broadcaster PJ Gallagher, who has died at the age of 51.
Born in Cork and adopted and raised in Dublin, Gallagher was a familiar presence on television for more than two decades, appearing in numerous programmes, including BBC's The Young Offenders.
He first came to prominence in 2005, co-creating the RTÉ hidden-camera series Naked Camera, which established him as one of Ireland's best-known comedy performers.
As well as his work in stand-up comedy and acting, Gallagher presented television documentaries and was a member of the breakfast show team on Radio Nova.
Posting on social media, Martin described Gallagher as a "gifted comedian, actor and broadcaster" who brought "immense warmth and laughter to so many across Ireland".

Gallagher's agency LR Comedy confirmed his death in a statement on Friday evening, saying his family and friends were "devastated" and asked that they be given privacy and time to come to terms with their loss.
The statement also highlighted how Gallagher spoke with "remarkable candour about his experiences of mental illness", wanting people to "talk about what they were going through without shame".
He published a memoir in 2023 titled Madhouse: The naked truth about my chaotic childhood, losing my mind and finding a place to call home.
Following this he made a documentary called Changing My Mind, which explored mental health issues.

More recently Gallagher headed the RTÉ One series The Random Driving Test, after participating earlier in the year in the second season of Uncharted with Ray Goggins, where he joined actor Liam Cunningham, and Goggins on a motorbike expedition across the Himalayas.
Gallagher's The Young Offenders co-star Alex Murphy said his heart was "broken" after learning of his death.
"I can't believe it. The relentlessly funny PJ Gallagher will be missed beyond belief," he posted on Instagram.
Hilary Rose, who plays Murphy's on-screen mother on the show, said it was difficult to "wrap her head" around Gallagher's death.
Writing on Bluesky, comedian Dara Ó Briain said Gallagher was "the sweetest soul; and a warm, instinctive, funny-bones performer".
Podcaster Blindboy Boatclub echoed Ó Briain's comments, describing Gallagher as an "incredibly sweet and kind person".
Liverpool comedian John Bishop also paid tribute, describing Gallagher as "funny, kind, caring, humble and vulnerable.
"My thoughts go out to his close friends and family and he will be in my mind whenever I get on my bike to clear my head."
In 2007, Gallagher won an Irish Film and Television Academy Award for his RTÉ series Naked Camera
Radio Nova, where Gallagher hosted the Morning Glory breakfast show with Jim McCabe, said he "will be so dearly missed by all who had the privilege to cross his path".
Steve Carson, Irish broadcaster RTÉ's Director of Video, said that Gallagher had "brought his extraordinary wit, warmth, empathy and energy to everything he did".
"We are saddened to hear of the passing of PJ Gallagher," said Chris Sussman, Director of BBC Comedy.
Sussman added he "will be fondly remembered for his role" in the BBC Three series The Young Offenders.
Tánaiste (Irish deputy prime minster) Simon Harris said he was "deeply saddened" by the news, describing Gallagher as a "true treasure of Irish broadcasting and comedy".
Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said she was heartbroken for Gallagher's family, describing him as "down-to-Earth and warm".

"A true blue-Dub, proud northsider, a passionate supporter of Dublin GAA and Bohemians. He loved this place. PJ had so much to give and he gave it with such spirit, generosity and glint in his eye," she said.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c60m: The prime minister's spokesperson has said broadcasters must "act responsibly" and that "we have no interest in hearing" what Huw Edwards has to say, following a backlash against new interviews with the disgraced former BBC News presenter.

Pressed on whether the prime minister believed Channel 4 had not acted responsibly, they said: "Channel 4 is editorially independent and decisions about individual programmes and contributors are a matter for them."

During the court case, Edwards admitted three counts of making indecent images of children. That involved having 41 images and videos, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, said it felt like the media companies were "not thinking about the victims in this particular case".
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvly: Gary Barlow, Mark Owen and Howard Donald said their 10th number one album felt as special as their first
Take That have landed their 10th number one album, securing their spot as one of the most successful British bands in Official Chart history.
The Manchester group, made up of Gary Barlow, Howard Donald and Mark Owen, topped the UK album chart with Dreamers.
The group first scored a number one record more than three decades ago with their second studio album Everything Changes.
The band told Official Charts: "Thank you so much to everybody who has supported Dreamers, it means the world to us to see people embracing this album.
"Thinking back to our first number one with Everything Changes in 1993, this one today feels even more special.
"The fact that we can still reach these heights after 30 years is a feat not lost on us, and we wouldn't be here without our incredibly dedicated fans."
Take That's 10th studio album also secured the biggest opening week for a group in 2026 so far, outselling the rest of the top 10 combined.
The band now tie with Queen and Coldplay as the groups with 10 number one albums, with only The Beatles and The Rolling Stones boasting more chart-topping LPs among British bands.
Take That (left to right Howard Donald, Gary Barlow, Mark Owen and Jason Orange) a week after announcing they were splitting up in 1996
They are also one of just five groups to have topped the Official Albums Chart in each of the past four decades, alongside Blur, Oasis, Stereophonics and Steps.
The group previously topped the charts in 2023 with This Life.
The British boyband, known for the songs Back For Good, Pray and Shine, rose to fame in the 90s, and also featured Robbie Williams and Jason Orange.
Williams left the group in 1995 to pursue a solo career and Orange left in 2014.
Asked how the band would be celebrating the album hitting the top spot, Barlow said: "Let's go to the seaside and get fish and chips - and an ice cream."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c920: Jamie Miller has equalled the six-week streak set by Dave Edmunds' I Hear You Knocking in 1970
Jamie Miller's Babydoll has become the longest-running UK number one single by a Welsh artist in 56 years.
Miller, who is originally from Pontprennau in Cardiff, claimed the top spot with his TikTok-viral hit for the sixth consecutive week on Friday.
The 29-year-old star's success is equal to the six-week streak set by Dave Edmunds' I Hear You Knocking back in 1970.
Babydoll was released on 7 August - just months after Miller considered quitting music - and exploded after actress Jennifer Love Hewitt and other stars posted videos which featured the track.
The song snowballed on social media and led to a viral dance, his first UK top 10 single , and reached number one in the US iTunes pop chart.
Miller is the first Welsh artist since 2011 to earn a UK Number 1 single - after Sian Evans' feature on DJ Fresh's Louder.
He is also the first solo male Welsh artist in 41 years to top the singles chart, after Shakin' Stevens' 1985 timeless festive hit, Merry Christmas Everyone.
Following the achievement, Miller said "nothing feels normal" anymore , but he was trying to "live in the moment" as he comes to terms with his history-making song.
The success transformed his career, but he said his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.
Miller, who grew up in Cardiff but has lived in Los Angeles for about nine years, launched his career nearly a decade ago as a 19-year-old, after coming third on the sixth season of The Voice UK.
He also recorded a separate version of Babydoll with Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano , after initially joking about the idea on social media.
Cipriano told BBC Wales Miller was "one of the best vocalists I've ever heard", adding he had been a fan of Miller's voice "for years".
Sir Elton John previously said he was "leaping around the kitchen" when he first heard Miller's history-making single.
Speaking on Sir Elton's Rocket Hour podcast, the Rocket Man singer told Miller he had a "huge future".
Jamie Miller (right) and Off Campus star Antonio Cipriano recorded a version of Babydoll together after a joke on social media
He said, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.
But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".
Miller said he was working on a "soulful, joyous and happy album that I feel like I've waited my whole life to write", and hopes it will be released at the beginning of 2027.
Last week, Miller released his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.
In addition, the singer is currently planning a world tour, with a promise to return to his roots and perform a number of shows in Wales.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c65y: Ant McPartlin and Dec Donnelly present the show and host their own podcast
I'm a Celebrity... Get Me Out of Here host Declan Donnelly has said tensions between Mariella Frostrup and AJ Odudu over cooking duties on the show "became a much bigger deal than it should have".

Co-host Ant McPartlin said "cooking makes things very tense in camp", adding: "If they could zoom out a little bit in there, they'll realise it's not that deep. But they just can't, once they're in there".

Donnelly and McPartlin discussed on their podcast how relations became fractious, when Odudu attempted to help Frostrup cook on Saturday's episode - the next day Odudu was distressed after Frostrup accused her of being "aggressive".
On Wednesday 887 people complained to Ofcom about Sunday's episode in relation to "alleged bullying behaviour" by Frostrup towards Odudu.
Wayne Rooney tried to repair relations between AJ Odudu (left) and Mariella Frostrup on Sunday

Frostrup apologised during an amicable conversation on Tuesday, and Odudu accepted, explaining it was "triggering" because "it's a strong word to use in casual scenarios, particularly towards black women".
On their podcast, Hanging Out with Ant and Dec, Donnelly said tensions in camp started "surprisingly early".
"From day one cooking was tense and then it obviously came to a head with AJ and Mariella, and it spilled over to breakfast the next morning," he said.
McPartlin added: "You have 12 hungry mouths to feed and you and your sous chef, the other chef, are cooking and everyone is stood around looking at them. The pressure is quite a lot."
Donnelly continued: "When you are there, and so much of your life revolves around that mealtime, it's the only meal of the day you really get that isn't rice and beans.
"There is a lot of pressure and obviously Mariella was feeling that pressure.

"AJ wanted to come in and help and it all came to a head, and maybe because there was so much pressure and because it was so important, Mariella maybe didn't handle it very well around the campfire when she was cooking, and it spilled over into the next day - and it became a much bigger deal than it should have done."

He said the "most important thing" was that "the two ladies were able to sit down and drew a line under it, they were adult enough to sit there, talk it through, and move on together. If more people did that the world would be a much better place".
McPartlin agreed, saying: "If some of our leaders did that, the world would be a better place."
AJ Odudu said being called aggressive was "very harsh" and it was "an insane word" to use about her
On Wednesday, an Ofcom spokesperson told BBC News: "We are assessing the complaints against our rules, but are yet to decide whether or not to investigate."
On Thursday night, Frostrup completed her fourth bushtucker trial, which is voted for by the public.

They included broadcaster and comic Judi Love who said she felt "triggered by Frostrup's comment, while Britain's Got Talent judge Alesha Dixon and Strictly Come Dancing judge Motsi Mabuse also gave their support to Odudu.
BBC Radio 1 DJ Clara Amfo said: "Calling a black woman 'aggressive' when she is being anything else but is a classic microaggression."

Speaking on spin-off show I'm A Celebrity... Unpacked on Sunday, former campmate Jordan Banjo said Frostrup had handled the situation "poorly", but urged people to "give a bit of grace to Mariella, and everyone in the camp" because "you can't judge an abnormal situation by normal standards".

It is "a really weird situation that every single person's in, and I'm not sure if people go at stuff with the clearest head", he said, explaining: "You get these weird breakdowns, and I think that's what we're seeing."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckp8: Ten songs from Grand Theft Auto 6 appear in the UK's Official Singles Chart top 100
Grand Theft Auto 6 has been swerving into online feeds and cultural conversations since its record-breaking launch last week.
But one area where the game is really making a dent is the world of music.

Flower In A Hurricane, the single from the game's official soundtrack album by Justice featuring Tame Impala, SZA and King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard, has climbed to number three on the UK's Official Singles Chart.
Go Easy, a new track from Dua Lipa specially recorded for the game, is the highest new entry at 21.
Seven other songs recorded for GTA 6 by artists including Lana Del Rey, Travis Scott and Morgan Wallen also placed in the top 100.
Video game music has topped the UK chart before, when Robbie Williams' It's Only Us, recorded for the FIFA 2000 soundtrack, got to number one.
Run Away With Me, a 2015 song by Carly Rae Jepsen used during a "needle drop" moment in the game's first chapter, has also seen a huge spike in listeners.
It originally peaked at number 58 in the UK 11 years ago, but has re-entered the charts at number 28.
Speaking to BBC music correspondent Mark Savage, Jepsen remembered feeling the track had "something special to it" when she recorded it.
While it's a favourite among some of the singer's most loyal fans, it has never reached the level of recognition as her hits Call Me Maybe and I Really Like You.
"It's just so lovely to see that happening, it makes me believe in that special feeling that we had."
Music plays a key role in the game, both inside and outside its storylines

There are three elements of GTA 6's soundtrack, including an official, double-sided album containing tracks recorded for the game, and an original score composed by electronic duo Justice, due to be fully released in December.
The game also features hundreds of licensed tracks on its in-game radio stations.
Flower In A Hurricane was released as a single in October, giving it time to appear on playlists in the lead-up to the game's debut.
But Mat Ombler, head of partnerships at video game music label Laced Records, says GTA 6's impact on the charts is still impressive.
He says video game soundtracks entering the album charts "isn't unheard of" but "it's incredibly rare to see multiple tracks hitting the singles charts".
Ombler likens the spike in streams of Jepsen's track to the boost Kate Bush's Running Up That Hill got from its inclusion in Netflix hit Stranger Things.

"Both tracks are part of a huge cultural moment, but I'd argue that GTA's usage of Run Away With Me is more impactful... where the music responds according to what you're doing during a key story mission," he says.
Ombler thinks the chart impact of GTA 6 highlights "the growing importance and cultural impact of video game soundtracks as a whole".
"Over 40 million people will spend the coming weeks and months listening to more than 800 tracks featured in the in-game radio stations, possibly hundreds of times," he says.
"They'll discover new music in genres they might never have engaged with otherwise, and this music will stick with them for the rest of their lives."
Electronic duo Fcukers appear on the official GTA 6 soundtrack
Only One by New York band Fcukers appears on the official GTA 6 soundtrack and has already had more than one million streams on Spotify.
The group's singer Shanny Wise tells Newsbeat: "It was actually one of the songs we recorded when we were making our album, but it didn't end up making the album."
"We felt like the vibe of it maybe was too much of an outlier," adds bassist Jackson Walker Lewis.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmn5: Veruschka was a distinctive presence on the covers of magazines like Vogue and Life in the 1960s and 70s
Veruschka, the model and artist who became one of the first global fashion stars in the 1960s, has died at the age of 87.
She became known as the striking subject of fantastical photoshoots that helped expand the boundaries of fashion and beauty in the 60s and 70s, appearing on the cover of American Vogue 13 times.

Vogue's obituary , external described her as "the shape-shifting supermodel who defined an era", explaining: "One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion's great performance artists."
She also made memorable appearances in classic swinging 60s film Blow Up and 2006 James Bond movie Casino Royale.
Veruschka was born Vera von Lehndorff into an aristocratic family in 1939 in Königsberg, then in Germany, now known as Kaliningrad in Russia.
Her father, Heinrich Count von Lehndorff, was executed in 1944 for his part in a failed plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler.
She studied art in Hamburg and Florence before beginning her career as a model "and soon became a legend", her sister Countess Catharina von Lehndorff wrote in a tribute , external .
"She worked with Yves Saint Laurent, Karl Lagerfeld, and Valentino, but also immersed herself in avant-garde photography projects in which she painted, staged, and deconstructed her body.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmp3: Watch: Taylor on the 'overwhelming reaction' to Duran Duran's music
Simon Le Bon, Sir Rod Stewart and Gary Kemp are among the pop stars who have paid tribute to Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor following his death at the age of 65.
Taylor co-wrote some of the group's biggest hits including Save A Prayer, Rio and Girls On Film.

Le Bon and his bandmates paid tribute, saying "he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music", while Sir Rod remembered his "dear pal" and Spandau Ballet's Kemp called him "a great player who set the tone for the 80s".

Taylor's wife Tracey called him "the rock of our family", adding: "We will miss him every single day." He died after "a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", Duran Duran said in a statement on Wednesday.
Andy Taylor: Duran Duran's livewire guitarist who was a Wild Boy on stage and off
He died "peacefully at home, surrounded by his family, on Monday 23rd November", a statement said.

Paying tribute, his Duran Duran bandmates said: "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."
They said their thoughts were with his wife, children and grandson.
Le Bon said there was a "a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart".
"Andy never took the easy musical route. His overdrive overdrove us into being the only funk/rock/punk band in the New Romantic movement, with songs that still survive, decades later."
Watch: Andy Taylor tells the BBC about his cancer diagnosis in 2023
Sir Rod, who wrote five songs with Taylor for the 1988 album Out of Order, recalled them making "some good music together" and having "some outrageous fun".
Kemp said Taylor "influenced many of us along the way with his sparse staccato style", adding: "He brought shameless rock to the mix."
In a band tribute, Spandau Ballet called him "a hugely talented musician and an important part of the British music scene".
US guitarist Nile Rodgers, the co-founder of Chic, recalled "countless great days and nights" with his "dear friend".
Belinda Carlisle said she was "blessed" to have worked with Taylor, who played the guitar solo and was in the video for her song Mad About You.

Former Led Zeppelin frontman Robert Plant called Taylor "a tough fighter", while Then Jerico's Mark Shaw remembered him as "one of the greatest musicians and songwriters I've ever heard and had the privilege to work with".
Taylor (second left) married his wife Tracey at the Chateau Marmont hotel in Los Angeles in 1982

Taylor's wife Tracey, a hairstylist he met during the early days of Duran Duran, and whom he married in 1982, said: "For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first for Taylor, adding: "Nothing made him happier than having us all together."

She said he faced the last few years "with so much courage and determination" and said they were "grateful" for the "kindness and support shown to him by fans throughout his illness", saying it brought him "immense comfort and strength".
Andy Taylor's guitar riffs powered some of Duran Duran's best-known songs
The son of a fisherman, Taylor taught himself guitar, bass, and drums and began playing professionally at age 13.
He played with several bands around the UK before answering a music paper advertisement for a "live-wire guitarist", which led to his audition for Duran Duran in Birmingham in April 1980.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjr: The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.
The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.
Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".
But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.
The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.
A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts
Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app
More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters
More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate
There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.
Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".
BBC weather bulletins will now include Met Office branding (presenter Matt Taylor pictured)

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."
A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.
Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.
Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.
Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.
The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.
The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.
A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c574: The former Wales captain says he wants to encourage more men to talk openly about hair loss.
Rugby legend Alun Wyn Jones has urged men to open up about hair loss, saying he was "very comfortable" talking about the fact he has had a hair transplant.
Speaking one year since his operation, the former Wales and British and Irish Lions captain said men typically do not talk about the issue, but said "a lot of people" had spoken to him about it.
"I think it's important that people know there's a lot of people out there they can talk to," he said.
Jones played 158 times for Wales and 12 for the Lions, making him the most capped rugby player in history before he retired in 2023.
Jones, 41, from Swansea, said he "wasn't conscious" about his hair loss until his playing days were coming to an end.
He spent most of his career playing for the Ospreys, before a stint for Toulon in France near the end of his career.
He said his playing career had prevented him from getting a transplant sooner because of the time off required after the procedure and then to "recover properly".
But after his retirement he said he began to learn more about it and had the operation.
He said he hoped his openness about hair loss would encourage other men to talk about the issue.
"Men in general don't talk, but I've had a lot of people talk to me about it," he said.

Male pattern baldness , external (androgenetic alopecia) is a genetic form of hair loss, with signs of recession usually beginning in the teenage years with "prevalence and severity" increasing with age, according to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) , external .
It said that, in general 30% of white men are affected by 30, 50% by 50, and 80% by 70. Prevalence is highest in Caucasians.
Jones says he did not have the time for the procedure during his playing career
Since retiring from rugby, Jones has become an ambassador of 3rd Battalion, the Royal Welsh , the Army's only reserve infantry regiment in Wales, and has documented his efforts to learn Welsh.
Jones, whose wife and three daughters all speak Welsh at home, said learning the language was about "knowing my roots and belonging to my country".
He also competed in the 20th series of Celebrity MasterChef and finished as a runner-up.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly: Gérard Depardieu has faced a series of allegations in recent years on film sets and elsewhere
French film actor Gérard Depardieu is to stand trial for the alleged rape of actress Charlotte Arnould, a Paris appeals court has confirmed.
Arnould, who was 22 at the time, had reported the alleged rape several days after going to his house in Paris to rehearse a play.
She has waived her right to anonymity and her lawyer said Thursday's ruling was a "first" and the forthcoming trial would be historic.

Depardieu, 77, had contested his indictment on two counts of rape. In a letter published in Le Figaro in 2023, Depardieu strongly denied Arnould's allegations, saying "there was never any coercion or violence between us".

Depardieu was for decades a leading figure in French and international cinema for roles in Green Card, The Man in the Iron Mask and the Asterix films. He was awarded France's Légion d'honneur in 1996.

But in recent years a series of allegations have been made against him over his conduct on film sets and elsewhere in the wake of France's #MeToo movement, known as balance ton porc ( call out your pig).

Last year, he was given an 18-month suspended jail term after he was found guilty of sexually assaulting two women on a film set in Paris in May. He was also placed on the sex offenders register and ordered to pay compensation.
He dropped his appeal against the ruling last week and offered "sincere apologies" for his behaviour on the set of director Jean Becker's 2021 film Les Volets Verts (The Green Shutters).
Depardieu had been a friend of Charlotte Arnould's father and on 7 August 2018 she had gone to his home, where much of what happened was captured on the actor's own CCTV.
Arnould's case was initially dismissed for insufficient evidence, but after she filed a civil complaint, a judicial investigation was opened in the summer of 2020.
Speaking outside the Paris appeal court on Thursday, her lawyer Carine Durrieu Diebolt said the ruling was a victory for her client for whom it was "genuinely a relief".
The appeal court said that while Depardieu should stand trial for what took place on that day, he would not be tried for a further alleged rape at a hotel six days later.

Depardieu's lawyer David-Olivier Kaminski told reporters that court had partly ruled in his favour: "As soon as we get the ruling, we will look into the possibility of appealing to the Court of Cassation."
Meanwhile, Depardieu is under a separate investigation alongside French author Michel Houellebecq for "allegations of a sexual nature".
French authorities confirmed their inquiry last week, following reports of an alleged "gang rape" on the set of the film Thalasso in 2018.
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmvg: Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.
"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.
They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62 , argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.
The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.
"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".
The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.
It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.
Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.
Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.
Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.
Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.
They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.
It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.
At the time of their 2014 marriage, Pitt and Jolie were among the most lucrative names in Hollywood.
They met on the set of the 2005 film Mr and Mrs Smith and were soon dubbed Brangelina by the press.
The marriage was Pitt's second after a relationship with Friends star Jennifer Aniston.
It was Jolie's third, after actors Billy Bob Thornton and Jonny Lee Miller.
Jolie adopted her first child, Maddox, from Cambodia in 2002 a few months after he was born. Pitt later adopted him after he and Jolie had begun their relationship.
In 2005, the pair adopted daughter Zahara from Ethiopia when she was a few months old.
The couple's first biological child, Shiloh, was born in Namibia in 2006.
Their son Pax was adopted at the age of three from Vietnam in 2007, and twins Knox and Vivienne were born in 2008.
Since the couple split, four of the six children have legally changed their last name to Jolie rather than Jolie-Pitt, according to court filings citied by Hollywood press.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw5y: Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.
Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form – two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.
The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.
And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.
For decades, pharmacists have usually had to provide exactly the medicine prescribed by a doctor under rules set out in the 1968 Medicines Act.
If a product was out of stock, patients often had to return to their GP for an alternative prescription or wait for new supplies to arrive, if it was safe to do so.
Now, pharmacists will be able to make some tweaks without sending patients back to the doctor, including:
supplying the same dose of a drug in different strength pills
supplying the same medicine in a different form, such as a capsule rather than a solid tablet
The changes will apply across the UK once they have been approved by the relevant parliaments and assemblies.
Public health minister Diana Johnson said the new flexibility would make life easier for patients.

"When you go to the pharmacy to pick up your prescription, there is nothing worse than being told you need to contact your GP again because the exact medicine they've prescribed isn't available at that time, or in that form," she said.
"That's why we're changing the rules so that people can get the treatment they need with less hassle, and no delay."

The move follows a broader expansion of pharmacy services in England, which has given pharmacists greater powers to prescribe certain medications themselves without patients needing to see a GP at all.
Many other medicines, like certain painkillers and cold remedies, can also be bought over the counter at pharmacies without a prescription.
Henry Gregg from the National Pharmacy Association welcomed the move, but called for more action on drug shortages which he said were becoming endemic.
"These measures are a step forward but do not fix the underlying causes of shortages," he added.
"It's clear the government undervalues medicines, including underfunding vital local pharmacies.
"It must take action so that manufacturers don't favour other countries when stocks are low internationally."
The changes are separate from existing powers used during widespread medicine shortages.
If the government is concerned about national stocks of a particular medicine or medical product, it can still issue a Serious Shortage Protocol , external .
The measure has previously been used during shortages of some hormone replacement therapy (HRT) products, for example.
In those circumstances, pharmacists can already dispense an alternative without having to contact a GP first.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq8e: Health officials are urging more people to take up the offer of a free flu vaccine as the number of hospital patients seriously ill with the virus has risen sharply in the past week.
The flu surge has come slightly early this year but that is not completely unusual.
Flu activity is still at "moderate levels" and the peak may not arrive until December or early January, health officials warn.
So what is the advice on getting a vaccine, who can get it for free and who should pay?
"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London.
"The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups – so as many as possible should have it in those groups.
"People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."

Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill – complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.
In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.
Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter.
The current one protects against three strains – two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.
Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.

Millions of vulnerable people are eligible for the free jab to help protect them against flu, including children, pregnant women, care home residents, people with lung conditions and anyone aged 65 and over.
But only around a third of under-65s and two-thirds of those aged 65 and over have been vaccinated so far this winter.
That leaves around seven million people unprotected at present, health officials say.
Parents are being urged to vaccinate young children in order to protect them and other people they come into contact with.
Yes. The vaccine does not rule out the possibility you will get flu, but it does reduce the chances you'll become very ill with it and end up in hospital.
It takes two weeks for your body's immunity to build up after being vaccinated, which is another reason to have the jab sooner rather than later.
Protection from the vaccine reduces the risk of serious flu complications by 50%, says Prof Hopkinson.
If you are not eligible for the free flu vaccine, you can still buy it from most pharmacies for between £15 and 25.
But it is far more important for the millions of vulnerable people offered it free to be vaccinated.
They are known to be at risk of health complications from the virus.
Other groups are also at risk: "Smokers are five times more likely to get flu – so quit now," he suggests.
There are different vaccines for those getting it free on the NHS and those paying for it privately.
However, the vaccines do the same job and protect against the same strains of flu.
Pharmacist Olivier Picard says he's seen a "massive spike in demand" for flu jabs in the last 24 hours.
More people are booking an appointment for a free vaccine they have already been reminded about, and others are asking about paying for it themselves.
"When it gets cold, people tend to wake up to getting the free jab and want it before Christmas," he says.
He says there is no issue with supplies of the vaccine at present and "plenty in the system".

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwvg: A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.
The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over was just under 68% - lower than where it usually was at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long-term health conditions.
Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, talked of how some hospitals had introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.
Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".
"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.
However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.
Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it."
Suzanna McDonald, who leads the UKHSA's flu programme, said the H1N1 strain was fueling the spread.
She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the strain "does seem to have picked up a few more changes that we would have expected over the season".
"But the really encouraging news was that last year when we saw a drifted strain, the vaccine still worked very well," she added.

Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.
"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."
Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.
Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.
Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.
Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.
But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.
School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.
McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.
"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw62: Reform UK is promising to scrap parking fees at NHS hospitals in England for all patients, visitors, and staff if it wins power at the next election.
The party said rising parking charges in recent years were unfair, with some hospitals charging up to £20 a day for parking spots.
It says it would compensate hospital trusts for the £300m they currently get from fees each year by raising more from foreign visitors using the NHS.
The health department said it expected charges to be reasonable, with fees used to maintain facilities or put towards funding health services.

Reform's announcement is part of a broader effort by the party to win credibility on the NHS, as it prepares to appoint someone who has worked in the NHS as its health spokesperson in the coming weeks.
Leader Nigel Farage's previous support for an insurance-based healthcare model has harmed the party's standing on the health service, insiders admit.

The latest policy is also part of a series designed to improve the party's recent struggles in the polls by addressing what Reform see as their perceived weaknesses, on Russia, on defence and now the NHS.

Reform's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick told the BBC the party's spending plans would be set closer to an election, but the party would ensure there would always be "real-terms increases" in funding for the NHS.
Echoing a line traditionally used by British politicians to claim stewardship of the health service, he said: "What we are saying is that the NHS is safe in our hands".
Parking at hospitals in Wales and Scotland is largely free, but NHS trusts in England are allowed to charge and set their own fees and rules.
Government guidance means parking is free for disabled people holding Blue Badges, frequent outpatients, parents of sick children staying overnight and NHS staff working night shifts.
But most visitors are generally expected to pay, along with staff working day shifts.
Reform says its policy to compensate NHS trusts would cost £285m a year to deliver, assuming a £25m annual saving from payment collection costs that would not longer be required.

It plans to recoup lost revenue by charging overseas visitors 200% of the national tariff for NHS services, instead of 150% currently, and extending charges to A&E visits, ambulance services and GP care.

It also says it would make all foreign visitors from countries that do not have reciprocal healthcare arrangements with the UK take out travel insurance covering NHS care, allowing it to "more aggressively collect" money due.

Siva Anandaciva, policy director at the King's Fund health think tank, said parking fees could be a "burden" for those visiting hospitals, but questioned whether Reform's proposals would raise enough to fully compensate trusts.

He said the additional charges on visitors for care would bring extra administration costs, whilst hospitals would need to spend money on systems to ensure free spaces were available to those who need them most.
The experience in Scotland had shown it can also take an "awfully long time" for hospitals to exit contracts with private firms running car pars, he said.
He added: "You might not end up saving as much money as you think".
The health department said it expected fees charged by trusts to be "reasonable and in line with the local area".
"Where charges do apply, the money made is used to maintain facilities, with surplus income put back into the NHS to benefit both staff and patients," a spokesperson added.

In response to parliamentary questions earlier this year, the department also argued , external fees were a "significant control mechanism" to manage capacity given the limited number of car parking spaces available.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c98r: The Competition watchdog says wide-ranging reforms are needed in the UK's private dentistry market to ensure people get a fair deal.
It says patients can struggle with costs and find it difficult to shop around and compare prices.
Around four million people did not go to the dentist in the past two years because they found treatment expensive, the watchdog estimates.
The British Dental Association says it is essential that there is a thriving private market but it is also vital that the government fixes NHS dentistry.

The Competition and Markets Authority's (CMA) interim report on private dentist services says millions of people are struggling with the costs of private dental care, with some delaying or going without treatment.
Private dentist services are now used by about 60% of UK patients for some care
At large dental groups prices rose by around 7% a year on average between 2023 and 2025, ahead of inflation and wage increases
A composite white filling is equivalent to about 36% of average weekly disposable income in the North East of England and 35% in Wales
There is wide variation in prices even in the same local area. In Preston, composite fillings ranged from £80 to £223
An amalgam filling (sometimes known as a silver filling) costs anything between £72 and £159 in Caerphilly
Lisa Frame, aged 64, from Norfolk, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that while her private treatment was very good, she felt resentful about the overall costs.
She needed three extractions, and a temporary and then permanent plate, costing around £2600.
"I am a retired lady but I do not receive a pension until I'm 67 and I have had to rely on my husband to help me.
"The dentist I have…has given a first class service but I still feel very resentful that I'd have had to pay so much money when I have made NHS contributions all my working life," she said.
Why is it so hard to find an NHS dentist? Find out how many have closed where you live
The report argues it is difficult for patients to shop around for a good deal, with one in six practices in the UK not publishing prices online.
The watchdog also says private dentists can have financial incentives to promote treatments and this can create a risk that patients are sold services not in their best interests.
There is also evidence that some practices have targets to switch NHS patients to private care.
The CMA says there can be substantial variation in profit margins between practices.
The UK has fewer dentists per person in the population than most European countries, with a high vacancy rate in practices and that can hold back the expansion of services.
The market isn't working well for dental patients according to Sarah Cardell, chief executive of the CMA.
"Many people are struggling with affordability, and those on lower incomes and in certain parts of the UK are hardest hit," she said.

"We're proposing a wide-ranging package of measures to change the way the market operates and will work with governments across the UK to finalise these recommendations ahead of our final report in March."

The British Dental Association (BDA) said it would work with the competition watchdog to come up with practical measures but said governments in the UK should make fundamental reforms to NHS dentistry.
Eddie Crouch, chair of the BDA, said: "It is essential that we have a thriving private dental market.
"But successive governments have left millions with no options when it comes to securing NHS care.
"When it comes to giving patients access to affordable care ministers hold almost all the cards."
A government spokesperson said "no one should have to choose between paying their bills and looking after their teeth" and said the government would carefully consider the findings of the report.
https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmly: Uganda is set to receive its first supplies of a cheaper version of a ground-breaking injection to prevent HIV, raising hopes of expanding access to the drug across Africa, where the burden of the disease remains highest.
The first global shipment of the generic drug, known as lenacapavir, arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with deliveries to Uganda expected in the coming days, the Global Fund has said.
The drug, administered as an injection twice a year, is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV infection and is expected to cost just $40 (£30) per person annually.
Zimbabwe is due to receive supplies early next year, with several other countries expected to follow.
The arrival of the generic drug comes just a year after the original version, developed by US pharmaceutical giant Gilead Sciences, became available in sub-Saharan Africa.
The original version cost about about $28,000 annually in the US, putting it beyond the reach of many of those in developing countries.
Focus on Africa podcast: Lenacapavir offering new hope for HIV prevention?
Lenacapavir works by targeting the protective protein shell of HIV, disrupting the virus's ability to multiply and establish an infection in the body.
In a landmark clinical trial involving more than 5,000 adolescent girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa in 2024, none of those who received the injection contracted HIV.
Health experts say the injection offers a major advantage over existing HIV prevention pills, known as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), which must be taken every day and can carry social stigma.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommended the drug for HIV prevention in July 2025 .
The Global Fund described the arrival of the drug in Africa as a "major breakthrough" in the fight against HIV, saying cheaper supplies would help reach millions more people at risk of infection.

"These deliveries mark an unprecedented acceleration and expansion in access to a highly effective, quality-assured generic HIV prevention medicine in low- and middle-income settings," the group said in a statement on Wednesday.
More than 189,000 people across 10 countries have already received their first injection of lenacapavir, according to the Global Fund.
The organisation expects 24 countries to have received supplies by the end of this year and, working with the US government, plans to reach at least three million people by the end of 2028.
It is eventually expected to be available in 120 low- and middle-income countries.
Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for nearly two-thirds of people living with HIV globally, with adolescent girls and young women disproportionately affected.
South Africa has the world's largest HIV-positive population, with nearly eight million people living with the virus. It is among the countries expected to receive the cheaper injection.
Some 41 million people worldwide were living with HIV last year, while 570,000 died from HIV-related illnesses, according to the WHO.

The rollout comes amid concerns that sweeping cuts to US foreign aid under President Donald Trump's administration could undermine decades of progress in tackling HIV in Africa, where many countries rely heavily on international funding for prevention and treatment.
